input.rationale: Reports the repeat of the multi-node experiment honestly (three cases reproduced identically, the authority witness did not because its precondition failed), states that precondition in the authority paragraph, and submits the revised experiment with a deterministic premise.

interpretations.rationale: Extension note: this successor reports the repeat of the multi-node experiment (receipt fe822d82c6264158826e0303b4ce59b1), which reproduced the commit-rule, durable-snapshot and availability cases with identical operands but not the authority witness, because the caller's persisted commit index was zero in that execution and the startup scan therefore recovered the configuration; the authority paragraph now states that precondition and the counterevidence records it. A revised experiment that holds the precondition explicitly is submitted with this batch. Extension note: this successor adds receipt 4178d9d5c479470cafb7ebd7951a9332, which observes in a three-voter group that a node recovering without a configuration never attempts candidacy while the same node and log with the replay disabled do; the sources, the three earlier executions, the knowledge uses, the conclusion and the remaining counterevidence are otherwise unchanged, and the counter about the observation window is strengthened with the new control's sample counts. Correction note: this successor differs from the previous account of this question only by a transcribed latency; the control's election is now stated as the receipt records it (19 polls at a 5ms interval, about 95ms), not from an earlier construction run. Everything else - sources, executions, knowledge uses, counterevidence and limitations - is unchanged. Recovery. Receipt 9a373c13725a42aa9f48f59c0f2f2f1c restarted four real single-voter prefixes on their retained stores with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs on and off: with the flag on and no snapshot the node recovered an empty configuration (event 2: no members at index 0, 268 polls without a leader) although its log holds the bootstrap configuration entry at index 1 (event 0), the flag-off control on the same prefix shape tracked that entry and elected itself (event 6), and with a snapshot taken before a committed AddNonvoter the flag-on node kept the snapshot's index-1 configuration instead of the log's committed index-7 configuration (events 10, 11) while the flag-off control recovered index 7 (event 15). Source side the mechanism is settled: restoreFromCommittedLogs stores the persisted commit index and calls processLogs with it (api.go:723-754), advancing lastApplied before NewRaft runs the scan that rebuilds tracked configuration state from max(snapshotIndex, lastApplied)+1 (api.go:602-621), so committed configuration entries at or below that bound never reach processConfigurationLogEntry (raft.go:1605-1624) and the FSM's ConfigurationStore is never read back. That state decides election eligibility (raft.go:225-246), quorum size (raft.go:1085-1094), the leader's commitment membership (raft.go:456-467, commitment.go:35-64) and vote admission. First consequence: receipt 79a9cc34b3ce42e197c384775efecc3a removed server C from {A,B,C} (event 2: committed configuration at index 5 with two voters), restarted A with the flag on while B was partitioned, and A tracked the snapshot's index-1 three-voter configuration containing C (event 3); A won the election counting C and committed 'stale-quorum-entry' at index 10 term 4 with apply_error null, its FSM applied it, B's log lacked that index and C's log held it at the same term (event 4). Since A's own match cannot form a majority of three and B had no transport path, the deciding acknowledgement can only have come from C: the entry was committed, applied and reported successful against a member set that is not a majority of the committed configuration. Authority attempt. Receipt 4178d9d5c479470cafb7ebd7951a9332 builds a three-voter group, commits three commands so the staged commit index is non-zero, restarts A over its own stores and reads its tracked configuration: with the replay enabled A tracks no configuration at all (event 15: latest_config_index 0, no members, staged commit index 4), and in 266 samples over 1500ms of hearing no leader with the other voters shut down it was a follower in every sample and never a candidate (event 16, comparison violated); with the replay disabled the same node and the same log recover the three-voter configuration (event 17: latest_config_index 1, three members) and the node was a candidate in 254 of 266 samples, ending in state Candidate (event 18, comparison holds). A node whose tracked configuration is empty therefore does not merely fail to win an election: it never attempts to acquire authority, so it cannot be the source of a new leader even when the surviving members could form a quorum with it. The precondition is visible in the same operand: the empty configuration appears when the caller's store reports a non-zero persisted commit index, because that index becomes lastApplied and pushes the scan above the log's configuration entry. The repeat of this experiment (receipt fe822d82c6264158826e0303b4ce59b1) makes the dependence explicit: there A's persisted commit index was 0, so restoreFromCommittedLogs left lastApplied at zero, the scan started at index 1, A recovered the three-voter configuration (event 15: latest_config_index 1 with three members although the replay was enabled) and it did attempt candidacy, 255 candidate samples in 267 (event 16), which is why that execution's comparison returned unknown rather than a witness. The same repeat reproduced the other three cases with identical operands: the commit-rule case again tracked the snapshot's three-voter configuration against a log whose configuration entry has two voters and again committed with only the removed server's acknowledgement (events 2, 3, 4), the durable-snapshot case again wrote an empty configuration at index 0 into the snapshot metadata and again came up empty after a flag-off restart (events 6, 7, 8), and the availability case again committed with two members live and lost the ability after the second stop (events 11, 13). Second consequence, durable: receipt c477da09810f4842ba55130320e2a6b5 leaves A in that recovered state on a three-voter cluster (event 6: latest_config_index 0 with no members and committed_config_index 0, against its log's index-1 three-voter entry and staged commit index 4), takes a snapshot through the library's normal path, and reads back metadata recording no configuration at index 0 while the log establishes a three-voter configuration at index 1 (event 7, snapshot_config_matches_log_config false). A then restarts on the same stores with the replay disabled and comes up with an empty configuration at index 0, no leader within 1500ms, in state Follower (event 8). The loss is therefore not confined to the replay path: once written, the snapshot metadata re-imposes it on a restart that never enables the feature. Defect account: with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled and a commit-tracking log store, NewRaft cannot roll the node's tracked membership configuration forward past max(snapshot index, persisted commit index), so the node may keep an older or empty membership although its own log already contains the committed configuration entries; the recovered node can be permanently unable to participate, can decide leadership and commit index from a member set the committed configuration does not match - committing an entry a real voter of that configuration does not hold - and can write the lost configuration into durable snapshot metadata, from which later restarts, including ones with the feature disabled, restore it. The library's own test for the feature (raft_test.go:1183-1270) restarts with a snapshot whose configuration already equals the final configuration and asserts only the applied index, so it does not constrain this path. The failed first execution of the multi-node experiment (receipt 4ed46b198c8d41618cc855df0a63d469, exit 1) is retained in the run's logs but is not cited as an execution here: it stopped in the harness at the snapshot step because the elected leader was not the node being snapshotted, so it produced no comparison result about the target.

knowledge.assertion: The startup configuration scan runs from max(lastSnapshotIndex, lastApplied)+1, so entries at or below that bound never reach processConfigurationLogEntry at startup.
restoreFromCommittedLogs stores the store's commit index and calls processLogs with it only when the flag is set, which advances lastApplied to that index before the scan runs.
processConfigurationLogEntry is the only writer of the tracked configuration state; FSM-side configuration storage does not feed back into it.
The tracked latest configuration feeds quorumSize, the leader's commitment membership, leader-lease voter counting and the vote-admission checks.
A follower with configurations.latestIndex equal to 0 does not start an election, which is terminal when no reachable peer can supply a configuration entry.
Snapshots record the committed configuration and its index that the node currently tracks, and startup restores that metadata into the tracked configuration.

counterevidence: The doc comment for RestoreCommittedLogs (config.go:243-254) promises only that committed logs are replayed to catch the FSM up and says nothing about membership recovery, so the stale tracked configuration can be read as an unnamed side effect of a feature that never claimed to preserve it. The counter is that the startup scan at api.go:610-621 exists to rebuild that state from the log, and the observed consequences are a commit decided against a member set the committed configuration does not contain and a durable record that re-imposes the loss.

The commit-rule violation needs the removed server C to stay reachable after its removal, since its acknowledgement is what the stale majority counted; if it were stopped or unreachable the same stale configuration would instead leave the node unable to commit. The receipt therefore shows one reachable-removed-server case rather than every case.

One could argue the snapshot in the durable-state case is only as good as the state the node tracks, and that a caller should not snapshot a node whose configuration is empty. The counter is that the node is an ordinary cluster member whose own log contains the configuration entries, nothing in the API or the documentation marks its snapshots as unusable, and the resulting metadata then defeats a restart that has the feature disabled, so the corruption outlives the condition that created it.

The flag-off restart's failure to lead could be attributed to the 1500ms observation window rather than to the empty configuration. The counter is the source guard that refuses elections while configurations.latestIndex is zero (raft.go:225-241) plus two controls inside the same window: the single-voter control elected itself in 19 polls of the harness's 5ms interval (receipt 9a373c13725a42aa9f48f59c0f2f2f1c, event 6), and in the authority case the node that recovered its configuration was a candidate in 254 of 266 samples while the node with the empty configuration showed zero candidate samples (receipt 4178d9d5c479470cafb7ebd7951a9332, events 16 and 18).

The harness assigns roles deliberately (A restarts, B is partitioned, leadership is moved with the library's transfer) and it takes the snapshot explicitly rather than through the automatic cadence. Those choices select the scenario but do not supply the stale or empty configuration, which event 6 shows against the node's own log, nor the acknowledgement, which C's log carries.

The first execution of the multi-node experiment failed in the harness before any comparison (receipt 4ed46b198c8d41618cc855df0a63d469) and is retained as a harness artifact; the later receipts contain the same scenario with both defects exercised.

The authority case removes the other voters by shutting them down, so it shows that the defective node never attempts candidacy; it does not show an outage that a correct recovery would have prevented, because the recovered three-voter configuration also lacks a quorum with one voter left. What the receipt adds is the capability difference, not a counterfactual outage.

The authority witness depends on a property of the caller's store: A's persisted commit index must be non-zero, because that value becomes lastApplied and pushes the startup scan above the log's configuration entry. The repeat shows the other side of that condition - with a persisted commit index of 0 the scan starts at index 1, A recovers its configuration and does attempt candidacy (receipt fe822d82c6264158826e0303b4ce59b1, events 15 and 16). The claim is therefore bounded to restarts whose store reports a non-zero commit index, which the original receipt's operand (staged commit index 4) shows for its own execution.
limitations: All nodes are in-memory transports and stores in one process and the harness uses a test log store whose staging is not atomic with its log writes; the caller-side durability contract of CommitTrackingLogStore is assumed, not verified, and no production store or snapshot store is exercised.

The durable-state case snapshots a node that has no snapshot on its stores and then restarts with the replay disabled; shipping such a snapshot to a follower, or corruption arising from the automatic snapshot cadence, is not exercised, and deleting the corrupt snapshot is not tested as a recovery.

The multi-node case is one prefix shape with one committed removal, keeps the removed server running, and injects no message loss, reordering or crash, so the decision defect is observed under a clean transport.

Schedule variation is limited: the multi-node scenario appears in two receipts with the same operands, the durable-state scenario in one, and the observation windows are 1500ms for non-participation and 2000ms apply timeouts.

The authority witness has one execution in which its premise held and one repeat in which it did not, so it is currently a single valid witness; a revised experiment that keeps committing until A's persisted commit index is non-zero was submitted with this batch and its receipt is not yet part of this account.
interpretations.joint_history: All four receipts are executions of this investigation's fixed experiments on the same captured source revision, in separate workspaces with no shared mutable state. Receipt 9a373c13725a42aa9f48f59c0f2f2f1c established the recovery behaviour on four single-voter prefixes; receipt 79a9cc34b3ce42e197c384775efecc3a exercised the same recovery as the setup of a three-voter cluster and observed the commit-rule consequence; receipt c477da09810f4842ba55130320e2a6b5 contains both that three-voter scenario again (events 0-4, with the same operands: a restart tracking the snapshot's index-1 three-voter configuration against a log whose newest configuration entry is index 4 with two voters, and a commit at index 9 completed with only the removed server's acknowledgement) and the new durable-state scenario (events 5-8, where the same recovery leaves an empty tracked configuration). The repeated scenario reproduces the earlier witness with fresh addresses, so the premises each receipt relies on are observed more than once and the newer receipts only add consequences. Receipt 4178d9d5c479470cafb7ebd7951a9332 uses the same three-voter construction as receipt 79a9cc34b3ce42e197c384775efecc3a and reports the same tracked-configuration operands (latest index, voter count, member ids) after a replay-enabled restart, with the replay-disabled restart of the same node and log as its control. Receipt fe822d82c6264158826e0303b4ce59b1 is the same fixed experiment as receipt 4178d9d5c479470cafb7ebd7951a9332 executed a second time in a fresh clean copy, which is why its events carry the same names and indices; the authority case is where the two differ, and the difference is the operand staged_commit_index, 4 in the first execution and 0 in the repeat.

scope.description: Same four cases as the predecessor harness with one change: before A is restarted in the authority case the harness commits further commands through the leader until A's commit-tracking store reports a non-zero persisted commit index, then restarts A and samples its state as before. The extra applies are reported as premise_filler_applies.
assumptions: A's persisted commit index is what restoreFromCommittedLogs reads at startup and it advances when A's log store stages a write, so more leader commits make it non-zero.
The premise loop is bounded and the case fails loudly if twenty further applies do not raise the value.
The rest of the authority case is unchanged: A restarts over its own stores with the case's replay setting, the other voters are shut down, and A's state is sampled every 5ms for 1500ms.
excluded: No change to the other three cases in the harness.
No assertion about winning an election; the observation remains the candidate attempt.

experiment.prefix: For each case the harness builds three assuranceMultiNode values, wires them, bootstraps the three-voter configuration and starts each node with a fresh MockFSM. It commits three commands through the elected leader, then keeps committing until A's commit-tracking store reports a non-zero commit index (at most twenty further applies, reported as premise_filler_applies), records that index and shuts A down. A new transport on A's address is connected to B and C, NewRaft is called on A's stores with a fresh MockFSM and the case's replay setting, and the harness reports A's tracked configuration. B and C are then shut down and A's state is sampled every 5ms for 1500ms, reporting follower, candidate and leader sample counts, whether candidacy was attempted and the final state.
experiment.responsibility: raft's startup recovery is responsible for establishing the configuration the log already contains, and whether it does so depends on the persisted commit index the caller's log store reports, which this harness now establishes explicitly before testing the voter's ability to attempt authority.

comparisons.description: With the premise held explicitly - a non-zero persisted commit index at A's restart - a voter whose log establishes the configuration must still attempt candidacy once the other voters are gone.
Control: the same node with the same log restarted with the replay disabled recovers its configuration and attempts candidacy.

experiment.revision_reason: The repeat showed that the authority case's premise is not guaranteed: A's persisted commit index can be zero at restart, in which case the startup scan recovers the configuration and the witness conditions do not arise. The revised harness keeps committing through the leader until A's store reports a non-zero commit index before restarting A, and reports how many extra applies that took.

scope.description: Restart a single-voter raft node on top of its own retained stores, once with RestoreCommittedLogs enabled and once with it disabled, on two prefix shapes: a prefix with no snapshot, and a prefix whose snapshot precedes a committed configuration change. Report the recovered configuration (index, membership) beside the newest configuration entry in the node's own log, and whether the restarted node reaches leadership inside a 1.5s window (30 election/heartbeat timeouts at 50ms).
assumptions: The prefix runs with RestoreCommittedLogs enabled so that the commit index is staged into the commit-tracking log store; otherwise a restart with the feature enabled reads 0 and the scan start would equal the snapshot index.
The restarted node keeps the same address and ID as the prefix, so the configuration recorded in its log and snapshot still refers to it.

The FSM is an in-memory MockFSM and a fresh instance is used for each restart, which is the mode the feature targets; the FSM state is therefore rebuilt from the snapshot plus the replayed committed logs.

InmemCommitTrackingStore is a test facility whose StageCommitIndex does not share a write with StoreLogs; the probe uses it only as the store that exposes a persisted commit index and does not claim its durability properties.
excluded: No multi-node cluster, partition, or crash of a leader is exercised, so the commit-loss consequence of a stale member set is not measured here.
No snapshot-on-start or FSM-implemented ConfigurationStore variant is exercised.
No production log store (for example a bolt-backed store) is exercised; the caller-side durability contract of CommitTrackingLogStore is assumed, not verified.

basis.prefix: Each case calls assuranceBuildPrefix: NewInmemTransport with a fresh random address; inmemConfig with LocalID = 'server-' + address and RestoreCommittedLogs = true; NewInmemCommitTrackingStore, NewInmemStore and NewInmemSnapshotStore; BootstrapCluster with a single Voter server at that address; NewRaft with a fresh MockFSM. The prefix then waits for real leadership through the normal election path, applies four LogCommand entries, and for the snapshot cases takes a real Snapshot, then issues AddNonvoter for a peer that never connects (committed by the single voter) and applies two more commands. GetCommitIndex, LastIndex and a per-index log scan record the persisted commit index and every configuration entry with its index and membership, then Shutdown closes the node. The case then creates a new transport bound to the same address, copies the config with RestoreCommittedLogs set to the case value, and calls NewRaft with the same log store, stable store, snapshot store and a fresh MockFSM. It polls State() every 5ms for 1500ms, then asks the main thread for the tracked configurations through r.configurationsCh (the same channel takeSnapshot uses) and reads snapshot index, AppliedIndex, CommitIndex and LastIndex.
basis.responsibility: raft's NewRaft is responsible for re-establishing the node's membership configuration from the node's own durable state before any election or quorum decision is made; the caller is responsible for supplying a log store whose GetCommitIndex is atomic with StoreLogs and for enabling RestoreCommittedLogs deliberately.

comparisons.description: A node restarted with RestoreCommittedLogs on top of stores whose log holds a committed configuration entry must still be able to elect a leader inside the observation window.
Control: the same prefix shape restarted with RestoreCommittedLogs off reaches leadership, which shows the nonprogress is specific to the replay path and not to the prefix.
The configuration recovered at startup must equal the newest configuration entry in the node's own log (index and voter/nonvoter membership).
Control: with the feature off the same predicate holds on the same prefix shape.
After restarting on a snapshot that predates a committed configuration change, the recovered configuration must include that committed entry.
Control: the same snapshot-plus-configuration prefix restarted with the feature off does recover the committed configuration entry.

scope.description: Build single-voter prefixes whose committed log lies about 9000 entries above an absent snapshot, then restart each prefix with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs on and off, calling NewRaft in a goroutine and reporting whether it returned within 8000ms together with a stack sample of the blocked goroutine.
assumptions: The prefix runs with RestoreCommittedLogs enabled and a raised SnapshotThreshold so the commit index is staged into the commit-tracking log store and no automatic snapshot moves the replay bound.
The restarted node keeps the same address and ID as its prefix and uses a fresh in-memory MockFSM, so the whole committed log above the snapshot is replayed.
The observation window of 8000ms is used only to decide completion; the claim that the block persists comes from the source, since the channel's consumer is started only after the replay returns.
excluded: No lowered MaxAppendEntries case, so the proportional relation between the bound and MaxAppendEntries is source-derived and not measured.
No multi-node cluster, so member loss caused by a node that cannot start is not measured.
No production log store, and no store whose StageCommitIndex is atomic with StoreLogs.

basis.prefix: For each case, the harness builds its own prefix: NewInmemTransport with a random address, inmemConfig with LocalID = 'server-' + address, RestoreCommittedLogs true, SnapshotThreshold 1<<30 and SnapshotInterval one hour, plus NewInmemCommitTrackingStore, NewInmemStore and NewInmemSnapshotStore; BootstrapCluster with one Voter; NewRaft with a fresh MockFSM; wait for real leadership; then 9000 Apply calls, each waiting for its future. It records the store's commit index, last index, snapshot index and the computed batch count, then Shutdown. The case creates a new transport on the same address, copies the config with RestoreCommittedLogs set to the case value, and calls NewRaft in a separate goroutine. The main goroutine waits up to 8000ms for that call to return; if it does not, it samples all goroutine stacks with runtime.Stack and reports the excerpt around the first frame naming restoreFromCommittedLogs. If NewRaft returns, the harness waits up to one second for leadership, reports the state and then shuts the node down.
basis.responsibility: NewRaft owns completion of its own startup work, including the RestoreCommittedLogs replay it performs before returning; the caller cannot observe or interrupt a NewRaft call that has not returned, so any unbounded wait in that path is owned by the library.

comparisons.description: NewRaft must return for a node whose stores hold a committed log; a restart that replays more than the FSM channel can hold must not leave NewRaft waiting forever.
Control: the same prefix shape restarted with the replay disabled returns from NewRaft, which distinguishes the replay path from a property of the prefix.

scope.description: Restart single-voter prefixes with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled and Config.MaxAppendEntries 16, once with a committed log of about 1500 entries (94 replay batches, below the 128-slot capacity) and once with about 3000 entries (188 batches, above it), calling NewRaft in a goroutine and reporting whether it returned within 8000ms plus a stack sample of the blocked goroutine. The same harness also reruns the two 9000-entry default-batch cases of the predecessor so the earlier observations stay in one artifact.
assumptions: MaxAppendEntries 16 is a legal configuration (ValidateConfig only requires a positive value) and is applied to both the prefix and the restart, so the batch size is the same on both sides of the comparison.
SnapshotThreshold is raised so no automatic snapshot moves the replay range, and the prefix runs with the feature enabled so the commit index is staged into the commit-tracking log store.
The 8000ms window decides completion only; the permanence of a block comes from the source, since the channel's consumer starts only after the blocked call returns.
excluded: No production log store, no multi-node cluster and no case in which an automatic snapshot overshoots the bound.

The below-bound case is not expected to elect a leader, because the configuration-recovery defect of the sibling investigation is active on the same restart; this experiment only asserts that NewRaft returns, and the leadership observation is reported without being asserted.

comparisons.description: A replay that fits in the FSM channel (94 batches against capacity 128 at MaxAppendEntries 16) must let NewRaft return, which places the bound above 1500 replayed entries for this batch size.

With the same batch size and flag, a replay needing 188 batches exceeds the channel capacity, so NewRaft must still return; the pair with the below-bound case measures the bound as the product of batch size and channel capacity rather than the amount of log.

scope.description: Three in-memory voters A, B and C on one another's transports. A snapshots while {A,B,C} is committed; the leader then removes C, which commits against {A,B}, and commits three more entries. A is shut down and restarted with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled over the same stores, while B is disconnected from A and C. The harness reports A's tracked configuration, whether A wins the election, and for a command applied after that: the client result, A's commit and applied index, whether A's FSM applied the payload, and whether the entry is present in A's, B's and C's logs.
assumptions: The removed server C keeps running and keeps answering AppendEntries, which is what a removal without shutting the process down leaves in place; the harness does not simulate C being killed.

scope.description: Three in-memory voters A, B and C. A command is committed, A is shut down and restarted with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled and no snapshot on its stores, and the harness records A's tracked configuration and the newest configuration entry in A's log. A command is committed again so A's FSM has something to snapshot, A takes a snapshot through the normal path, and the harness compares the snapshot's recorded configuration and configuration index with the configuration entry in A's log. A is then shut down and restarted again with the replay disabled, and the harness records the configuration the node comes up with.
assumptions: A's stores hold no snapshot before the first restart, so the flag-on startup replays the committed log above index 0 and the scan is skipped.
The snapshot is taken through the library's normal snapshot path (user snapshot request handled by the snapshot goroutine), so nothing in the harness supplies the configuration it records.
The second restart uses the same stores with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs false and a fresh in-memory FSM, so the configuration can only come from the snapshot metadata and the log scan.
The flag-off restart is expected to run without a leader in the observation window because an empty configuration prevents the node from starting an election.
excluded: No multi-node partition and no commit-rule consequence in this case; the earlier multi-node experiment covers that.
No production snapshot store, no process-level restart, and no case in which a later configuration entry above the snapshot index repairs the tracked configuration.
The harness does not attempt to remove the corrupt snapshot, so recovery by deleting durable state is not measured.

basis.prefix: The harness builds three assuranceMultiNode values (random in-memory transport addresses, inmemConfig with RestoreCommittedLogs true, NewInmemCommitTrackingStore, NewInmemStore and NewInmemSnapshotStore per node), wires the transports pairwise, calls BootstrapCluster with the same three-voter configuration on each node and NewRaft with a fresh MockFSM each. It waits for a real leader, and if A won, moves leadership to B with LeadershipTransferToServer so that A can be restarted without stopping the cluster's leader. One command is committed and the harness waits until A's FSM has applied a command entry. A is shut down and a new transport on A's address is connected to B and C; NewRaft is called on A's stores with RestoreCommittedLogs true and a fresh MockFSM, and the harness records the tracked configurations through r.configurationsCh plus A's staged commit index, last index and newest configuration entry. One more command is committed and awaited in A's FSM, then A.Snapshot() is called and the harness reads the newest SnapshotMeta from A's snapshot store, comparing its Configuration and ConfigurationIndex with the log's configuration entry. A is shut down again, a further transport is created on the same address and connected to B and C, and NewRaft is called with RestoreCommittedLogs false; the harness records the restored snapshot index, the tracked configuration, the leader observation over 1500ms and the final state.
basis.responsibility: raft's snapshot writer is responsible for recording the committed configuration that the node's log establishes, and raft's startup recovery is responsible for establishing membership from durable state; a node that loses its configuration must not write that loss into the durable record other nodes and later restarts depend on.

comparisons.description: The configuration recorded in the snapshot metadata must be the configuration the node's own log establishes, not the empty configuration the recovery left behind.

A restart with the replay disabled must not come up without a membership configuration when its own snapshot and log establish one; a violating witness shows the loss is durable rather than confined to the replay path.

scope.description: Three in-memory voters A, B and C with Config.MaxAppendEntries 16 and no snapshots. A leader is chosen that is not A, about 3000 commands are committed so A's staged commit index sits about 3000 entries above its (absent) snapshot, and A is stopped. A is restarted over its own stores in a goroutine, in one case with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled and in the other with it disabled, and the harness waits up to 8000ms for NewRaft to return. It then commits one command while two members are live, stops the member that is neither the leader nor A, and commits one further command, reporting the client results.
assumptions: The committed log above A's absent snapshot exceeds 128 * MaxAppendEntries (3000 entries against a 2048-entry bound), so the flag-on replay needs more batches than the FSM channel can hold.
The leader is moved away from A with the library's own leadership transfer so that stopping and restarting A does not remove the group's leader.
The member stopped after the restart is chosen to be the one that is neither the leader nor A, so the surviving live voters are the leader plus A when A started, and the leader alone when A did not.
The restart uses a fresh in-memory FSM and the same stores, transport address and ID as before.
excluded: No production store, no process-level restart and no disk fault: the blocked member's process is alive but its NewRaft call never returns.
No case in which the blocked member recovers later, and no measurement of how long a caller would wait before giving up on NewRaft.
Only one extra member is stopped, so the comparison is between a two-member and a one-member live group.

basis.prefix: The harness builds three assuranceMultiNode values with random in-memory transport addresses, inmemConfig overridden with MaxAppendEntries 16, SnapshotThreshold 1<<30, SnapshotInterval one hour and RestoreCommittedLogs true, plus a NewInmemCommitTrackingStore, NewInmemStore and NewInmemSnapshotStore per node. The transports are wired pairwise, BootstrapCluster is called on each node with the same three-voter configuration, and NewRaft is called with a fresh MockFSM each. The harness waits for a real leader and, if A won, transfers leadership to B with LeadershipTransferToServer before continuing. About 3000 commands are applied through the leader, each waiting for its future, and the harness records A's staged commit index, log last index, snapshot index and the implied replay batch count. A is shut down, a new transport bound to A's address is connected to B and C, and NewRaft is called in a separate goroutine on A's stores with a fresh MockFSM and the case's RestoreCommittedLogs value; the main goroutine waits up to 8000ms, and on non-return samples all goroutine stacks and reports the excerpt around the first frame naming restoreFromCommittedLogs. The harness then applies one command through the leader while two members are live, shuts down the member that is neither the leader nor A, applies one further command, and reports both results plus the state of the restart.
basis.responsibility: NewRaft owns completion of its own startup work, and a group's fault tolerance depends on every configured voter being able to run: a member that never finishes starting is a member the group does not have.

comparisons.description: Where the restarted member never returned from NewRaft, stopping one further member must not cost the group the ability to commit, because a member that could have started should still be available; the companion commit_while_two_live_ok field records that the group was committing before that stop.

Control: with the replay disabled the restarted member returns and the surviving pair still commits after one member is stopped, which attributes the loss in the companion comparison to the member that could not start.

scope.description: Two single-voter prefixes at Config.MaxAppendEntries 16 with no snapshot, built so that their persisted commit index ends at 2049 and 2050. Each prefix is restarted with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled, NewRaft is called in a goroutine, and the harness waits up to 8000ms. Both events report the entries in the replayed range and, separately, the number of entries in that range that become commit tuples and the batches those tuples need.
assumptions: The prefix applies commands one at a time and stops as soon as the store's commit index reaches the target, and the harness reports the value it actually reached.
The tuple count is derived by scanning the replayed range for LogCommand, LogBarrier and LogConfiguration entries, which is what prepareLog accepts at the default protocol version 3.
No snapshot exists on either prefix, so the replay starts at index 1 and the whole range is delivered.
The block is judged by non-return within 8000ms plus a stack sample naming the replay frames; permanence comes from the source, since the channel's only consumer starts after the replay returns.
excluded: No production store, no multi-node group and no default SnapshotThreshold: the point of this case is the boundary in batches, not the reachability of the range under default settings.
Only two points are placed, one batch below and one batch above the capacity, so no finer scan of the edge is attempted.

basis.prefix: For each target the harness creates an in-memory transport and a commit-tracking log store, configures inmemConfig with RestoreCommittedLogs true, MaxAppendEntries 16, SnapshotThreshold 1<<30 and SnapshotInterval one hour, calls BootstrapCluster with the single voter and NewRaft with a fresh MockFSM, waits for real leadership, and then applies one command at a time, re-reading the store's commit index after each apply, until it reaches the target. It records the commands applied, the log's last index, the staged commit index, the number of tuples in the replayed range, the batches those tuples need and the entry-based count, then shuts the prefix down. The restart creates a new transport on the same address, copies the config with RestoreCommittedLogs true, and calls NewRaft in a separate goroutine on the same stores with a fresh MockFSM; the main goroutine waits up to 8000ms and, on non-return, samples all goroutine stacks and reports the excerpt around the first frame naming restoreFromCommittedLogs.
basis.responsibility: NewRaft owns completion of its own startup work; the size of the replay it performs is set by the entries that become commit tuples, so the caller cannot infer the reachable replay from the log's index range alone.

comparisons.description: A replay of exactly 128 delivered batches fills the channel without exceeding it, so NewRaft must return.

A replay of 129 delivered batches needs one more batch than the channel holds, so NewRaft must still return; the pair with the 128-batch case places the bound at the channel's capacity in delivered batches rather than at a count of replayed log entries.

scope.description: Two single-voter prefixes built with DefaultConfig values left in place: SnapshotThreshold 8192, MaxAppendEntries 64, SnapshotInterval 120s, with only Config.RestoreCommittedLogs and the node timeouts changed. Each prefix applies 12000 commands, reports the committed range above its newest snapshot and whether that range exceeds the bound of 128*MaxAppendEntries, then restarts with the replay on in one case and off in the other, waiting up to 8000ms for NewRaft.
assumptions: The workload is a burst: the harness applies each command as fast as the in-memory stack allows, which is what a node whose write rate outpaces its snapshot cadence experiences.
The automatic snapshot loop wakes on a randomized timeout of up to SnapshotInterval, so the committed range above the newest snapshot can sit above the bound between checks.
The prefixes report whether any snapshot existed at restart, so the receipt shows whether the boundary condition held rather than assuming it.
The bound is the FSM channel's capacity of 128 batches times MaxAppendEntries commit tuples, which is what the earlier boundary experiment placed exactly.
excluded: No steady-state measurement of how long a node spends above the bound, and no production store, process-level restart or multi-node group.
No case in which an automatic snapshot fires during the burst; the receipt reports the snapshot index and the number of listed snapshots so a fired snapshot would be visible as a different setup.

basis.prefix: For each case the harness creates an in-memory transport, sets Config.LocalID and RestoreCommittedLogs true on inmemConfig (which overrides only the heartbeat, election, lease and commit timeouts), and leaves SnapshotThreshold, SnapshotInterval and MaxAppendEntries at their defaults. BootstrapCluster seeds the single voter and NewRaft starts the node with a fresh MockFSM; the harness waits for real leadership and then applies 12000 commands, each waiting for its future. It records the store's commit index, the log's last index, the last snapshot index, the number of snapshots listed, the three default parameters, the committed range above the snapshot and whether that range exceeds 128*MaxAppendEntries, then shuts the node down. The restart creates a new transport on the same address, copies the config with RestoreCommittedLogs set to the case value, and calls NewRaft in a separate goroutine on the same stores with a fresh MockFSM; the main goroutine waits up to 8000ms for it to return and, on non-return, samples all goroutine stacks and reports the excerpt around the first frame naming restoreFromCommittedLogs.
basis.responsibility: NewRaft owns completion of its own startup work, and the size of the replay it performs is set by how far the committed log has advanced beyond the newest snapshot; the library's default snapshot cadence is part of what determines that distance in normal operation.

comparisons.description: Where the committed range above the newest snapshot exceeds the bound with the library's default snapshot settings, a restart with the replay enabled must still return; the companion fields record the range, the bound and whether any snapshot existed.

Control: the same default configuration and the same committed range with the replay disabled returns from NewRaft, which attributes the non-return in the companion case to the replay rather than to the prefix.

scope.description: Three in-memory voters A, B and C. A leader is chosen, three commands are committed so A's staged commit index is non-zero, A is stopped and restarted over its own stores in one case with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled and in the other with it disabled, and the harness records A's tracked configuration. The other two voters are then shut down, and the harness samples A's state every 5ms for 1500ms, reporting how often it was a follower, a candidate or a leader.
assumptions: The cluster configuration is stable, so no new configuration entry reaches A after its restart and its tracked configuration can only come from its own startup path.

A's stores hold no snapshot, so with the replay enabled the startup scan is skipped and A ends up with an empty tracked configuration; with the replay disabled the scan covers the log and A recovers the three-voter configuration.

Removing the other voters by shutting them down tests whether the surviving voter attempts candidacy, not whether it can win; with the recovered three-voter configuration A cannot win either, since its quorum is two.
The two cases use separate clusters built the same way, so the flag is the only difference.
excluded: No assertion about winning an election or about cluster availability; the observation is the candidate attempt itself.
No membership change after the restart, no partitioned-but-live peer, and no production store or process-level restart.

basis.prefix: For each case the harness builds three assuranceMultiNode values (random in-memory transport addresses, inmemConfig with RestoreCommittedLogs true and a fresh MockFSM per node), wires the transports pairwise, calls BootstrapCluster with the same three-voter configuration on each and NewRaft for each. It waits for a real leader and commits three commands through it, then records A's staged commit index and shuts A down. A new transport bound to A's address is connected to B and C, and NewRaft is called on A's stores with a fresh MockFSM and the case's RestoreCommittedLogs value; the harness reads A's tracked configurations through r.configurationsCh and reports the latest index, the voter count and the member ids. It then shuts B and C down, samples A's state every 5ms for 1500ms, and reports the follower, candidate and leader sample counts together with the last snapshot index and the final state.
basis.responsibility: raft's startup recovery is responsible for establishing the configuration the log already contains, and a voter's follower loop is responsible for attempting to acquire leadership when it stops hearing from a leader and its configuration allows it.

comparisons.description: A voter whose own log establishes the cluster configuration must attempt candidacy once it hears no leader and the other voters are gone; a violating witness shows a configured voter that can never become a candidate.

Control: the same node with the same log restarted with the replay disabled recovers its configuration and does attempt candidacy, which attributes the inertness in the companion case to the recovery path.

interpretations.rationale: Source trace. NewRaft restores the newest usable snapshot, then, only with RestoreCommittedLogs, reads the persisted commit index from the commit-tracking log store, stores it and calls processLogs with it (api.go:723-754); processLogs sets lastApplied to that index (raft.go:1296-1364). Only after that does NewRaft run the scan that rebuilds the node's configuration from the log, and that scan starts at max(lastSnapshotIndex, lastApplied) + 1 (api.go:602-621). With the feature off, lastApplied equals the snapshot index, so the scan covers every configuration entry in the log; with the feature on, lastApplied is the commit index, which for a node that committed entries above its newest snapshot is strictly larger, so every configuration entry at an index <= that commit index is skipped even though it is present in the node's log and was applied to the FSM. The skipped entries can only have been processed by processConfigurationLogEntry, the sole writer of the tracked configuration state, and its startup caller is exactly that scan; FSM-side configuration storage does not feed back into r.configurations (raft.go:1605-1624). The resulting configuration state is not inert: configurations.latestIndex == 0 makes a follower refuse to start an election (raft.go:225-241), and configurations.latest supplies quorumSize, the voter set counted by checkLeaderLease, the membership map used by the leader's commitment, and the inConfiguration/hasVote admission checks for vote grants (raft.go:456-467, 1085-1094; commitment.go:35-64). Two consequences follow directly: a node with no snapshot recovers an empty configuration and can never elect itself (no reachable producer of AppendEntries or configuration entries exists in a single-voter cluster), and a node with a snapshot recovers the snapshot's older membership, including a member set that omits an entry its log already committed. The existing test for this feature (raft_test.go:1183-1270) restarts with a snapshot whose configuration is identical to the final configuration and asserts only the applied index, so it does not constrain this case. The defect is scoped to deployments that enable RestoreCommittedLogs and use a commit-tracking log store; the intended duty is that the node recover the configuration its own log establishes, which the scan exists to do.
counterevidence: The doc comment for RestoreCommittedLogs (config.go:243-254) describes replaying committed logs to bring the FSM up to date and says nothing about configuration recovery, so one could argue that a stale configuration view is an unnamed side effect rather than a broken contract. The counter is that the scan at api.go:610-621 exists precisely to rebuild configuration state from the log at startup, and its start index is the only reason entries are skipped; no other path restores that state after the replay.

The skip also removes work: with RestoreCommittedLogs, configuration entries below the persisted commit index were already delivered to the FSM as commit tuples, so an FSM implementing ConfigurationStore has seen them. That does not restore r.configurations, which is raft's own decision input and is not derived from the FSM.
limitations: The predicate recorded here is source-derived; the fixed experiment for this question has been submitted with this batch and its retained receipt is not yet part of this account. A native local run of the same harness was used only to validate operands while constructing it and is not offered as evidence.

Both prefix cases restart a single-voter cluster on an in-memory transport with an in-memory commit-tracking log store, so the observation window (1.5s = 30 election timeouts) measures non-participation of that node, not of a multi-node cluster.

The stale-membership consequence for a leader's commit index is argued from the code path that builds the commitment from configurations.latest; no scenario in this batch partitions a multi-node cluster to show a commit decided by a member set that the committed configuration does not contain.

The persisted commit index is staged only on log writes (raft.go:1392-1405, 1553-1561), so its value in the stored prefix is not necessarily the highest committed index; this does not affect the ordering argument, since any staged value above 0 exceeds the snapshot index in these cases.

interpretations.rationale: Receipt 9a373c13725a42aa9f48f59c0f2f2f1c restarted four real single-voter prefixes (bootstrap, election through the normal path, client applies, shutdown) on top of their retained log, stable and snapshot stores, twice per prefix shape, with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs on and off, and observed each restarted node for 1500ms (30 election/heartbeat timeouts at 50ms, polled every 5ms). Comparison 0 (flag on, no snapshot) is violated by witness event 2: the node ended in state Follower, leader_observed false over 268 polls, with latest_config_index 0, latest_config_ids empty and latest_config_voters 0, while the same prefix's log holds LogConfiguration@1 with one voter (event 0) and the persisted commit index was 5 (event 1). Comparison 1 (flag off, same prefix shape) holds at event 6: leader_observed true, latest_config_index 1 and latest_config_ids equal to the log's entry. Comparison 2 (flag on) is violated by witness event 3: recovered configuration index 0 with no servers against log_last_config_index 1 and log_last_config_ids carrying the single voter. Comparison 3 (flag off) holds at event 7 with config_matches_last_log_config true. Comparison 4 (flag on, snapshot at index 6 followed by a committed AddNonvoter at index 7) is violated by witness event 11: recovered latest_config_index 1 with exactly one voter and zero nonvoters (the snapshot's committed configuration, snapshot_index 6 in event 8), while the node's own log's newest configuration entry is index 7 with voters 1 and nonvoters 1 including the added peer. Comparison 5 (flag off, same prefix shape) holds at event 15 with the recovered configuration at index 7 including that peer. The controls differ from the violations only in the flag, on prefixes built the same way, so the difference tracks the replay path and not the prefix shape. Source side, the mechanism is settled: restoreFromCommittedLogs reads the persisted commit index, stores it and calls processLogs, which advances lastApplied to it (api.go:723-754), and only afterwards does NewRaft run the scan that rebuilds tracked configuration state, starting at max(lastSnapshotIndex, lastApplied) + 1 (api.go:602-621). With the flag off lastApplied is the snapshot index and the scan covers the log; with the flag on it is the commit index, so committed configuration entries at or below it are never passed to processConfigurationLogEntry, the only writer of r.configurations (raft.go:1605-1624). The consequence recorded here is that the restarted node's decision state can be the snapshot's configuration or an empty one: with latest_config_index 0 the follower branch refuses to start an election (raft.go:225-241), which is terminal for the no-snapshot case because no reachable peer can ever send a configuration entry, and the stale view is what quorumSize, the leader's commitment membership and the vote-admission checks consume (raft.go:456-467, 1085-1094; commitment.go:35-64). Defect statement: with RestoreCommittedLogs enabled and a commit-tracking log store, NewRaft cannot roll the node's tracked membership configuration forward past max(snapshot index, persisted commit index), so a restarted node may keep an older or empty membership even though its log already contains the committed configuration entries; it can then be permanently unable to participate, or decide quorum from a member set that the committed configuration does not match. The duty is not documented as waived: the flag's doc comment speaks only about catching up the FSM (config.go:243-254) and says nothing about membership, while the startup scan exists precisely to rebuild that state from the log. The existing test for the feature (raft_test.go:1183-1270) restarts with a snapshot whose configuration already equals the final configuration and asserts only the applied index, so it does not constrain this path.

98ee8dfd5fac4b84915f91ed4b094bcf-gap-0.explanation: At startup only two inputs write the tracked configuration state, in this order: restoreSnapshot copies the snapshot's committed configuration and its index into both committed and latest (api.go:645-684), and the scan at api.go:610-621 replays processConfigurationLogEntry over log indices from max(snapshotIndex, lastApplied)+1 upward. The restored FSM is not a source: the ConfigurationStore interface is write-only from raft's perspective (fsm.go:110-119 invokes StoreConfiguration; nothing reads it back), so the log scan is the only input that can roll the tracked configuration forward through the log. This is corroborated by the retained receipt: in the two feature-on cases the recovered configuration was exactly the snapshot's committed configuration (event 11: index 1, one voter, no nonvoters) or the empty configuration (events 2 and 3: index 0, no servers), never the newest configuration entry in the node's own log (index 1 in the no-snapshot case per event 0, index 7 in the snapshot case per event 8).

98ee8dfd5fac4b84915f91ed4b094bcf-gap-1.explanation: Partially answered. The receipt shows one decision that the stale view changed outside the node: in the snapshot case with the flag on, the node reached leadership (event 10: final_state Leader, leader_observed true, commit_index and last_applied 10) while its tracked configuration was the snapshot's index-1 configuration with one voter and no nonvoters, not its log's committed index-7 configuration (event 11). That election was nevertheless still justifiable under the real committed configuration, because the omitted member was a nonvoter and the voting majority of both member sets is the local node, so the observed election is not yet a quorum formed from members the committed configuration excludes. A commit index advanced by a stale voter set, for example after a committed removal or a committed demotion, remains open and is not established by this receipt.

knowledge.assertion: The startup configuration scan runs from max(lastSnapshotIndex, lastApplied)+1, so entries at or below that bound never reach processConfigurationLogEntry at startup.
restoreFromCommittedLogs stores the store's commit index and calls processLogs with it only when the flag is set, which advances lastApplied to that index before the scan runs.
processConfigurationLogEntry is the only writer of the tracked configuration state; FSM-side configuration storage does not feed back into it.
The tracked latest configuration feeds quorumSize, the leader's commitment membership, leader-lease voter counting and the vote-admission checks.
A follower with configurations.latestIndex equal to 0 does not start an election, which is terminal when no reachable peer can supply a configuration entry.

counterevidence: The doc comment for RestoreCommittedLogs (config.go:243-254) promises only that committed logs are replayed to catch the FSM up and says nothing about membership recovery, so the stale tracked configuration can be read as an unnamed side effect of a feature that never claimed to preserve it. The counter is that the startup scan at api.go:610-621 exists to rebuild that state from the log, and the replay merely moves its lower bound; nothing else reconstructs it afterwards.

In the snapshot case the node with the stale configuration nevertheless became leader and committed its no-op (event 10, commit_index 10), so this receipt does not show a wrong decision in that scenario: the omitted member was a nonvoter, so the majority of both the stale and the real configuration is the local node. This limits the demonstrated harm to losing a committed membership change from the node's decision state, and leaves a quorum-based violation to the open gap.

One could attribute the no-snapshot non-leadership to the observation window rather than the empty configuration. The control on the same prefix shape elected in 17 polls (about 85ms, event 6) while the feature-on node sat at 268 polls with latest_config_index 0 (event 2), and with no peers in that scenario no producer of AppendEntries or configuration entries exists, so the state cannot change on any later timescale.

Configuration entries below the persisted commit index were also delivered to the FSM as commit tuples during the replay, so an FSM implementing ConfigurationStore has observed them. That does not restore r.configurations, which is raft's own decision input and is never read back from the FSM.
limitations: All four cases restart a single-voter cluster over an in-memory transport with an in-memory commit-tracking log store; the non-participation result is about that restarted node, not about cluster availability in a multi-node deployment.

The membership difference observed in the snapshot case involves a nonvoter, so no quorum arithmetic differed between the stale and the real configuration here; the quorum consequence is argued from the code paths that consume configurations.latest and remains the open gap.
No production log store is exercised; the probe relies on a store exposing a persisted commit index, and does not verify the caller-side atomicity contract of CommitTrackingLogStore.
One prefix per case; the receipt shows schedule-independent consistency across two independent prefix constructions per shape, but not repetition of the same prefix.

The persisted commit index is staged only on log writes (raft.go:1392-1405, 1553-1561), so the value read at restart need not be the highest committed index; in these cases it is 5 and 8 respectively, both above the relevant snapshot index, which is the only ordering the argument uses.

interpretations.rationale: Source trace. With Config.RestoreCommittedLogs set, NewRaft reads the persisted commit index and calls processLogs with it (api.go:723-754). processLogs walks from lastApplied+1 to that index, accumulating commit tuples and flushing a batch whenever the batch reaches config.MaxAppendEntries, delivering each batch through a select that waits for r.fsmMutateCh or r.shutdownCh (raft.go:1302-1312, 1336-1350). fsmMutateCh is created with capacity 128 (api.go:560) and is consumed only by runFSM, which NewRaft starts after the replay returns (api.go:636-638). At startup lastApplied is the restored snapshot index, so the replay spans the committed log above the snapshot, and the number of sends is ceil((commitIndex - lastApplied)/MaxAppendEntries). With the default MaxAppendEntries of 64 that is 128 sends at 8192 entries, so any restart whose committed range above the snapshot exceeds 8192 entries blocks inside NewRaft on the 129th send, with the FSM goroutine not yet started, no timeout, and no reachable way to close shutdownCh because the caller has not received the Raft object. The trigger is a legal configuration or workload: a smaller positive MaxAppendEntries lowers the bound proportionally, and a node that has never snapshotted (or whose snapshots lag its write rate) exceeds the default bound without any tuning. The failure is a startup liveness failure, not a wrong decision: the node never begins participating, so a single-voter group stays down and a larger group loses one member permanently. No repair is enabled in the blocked state: the only escape from the send is a shutdown channel that only a caller holding the returned object could close.
counterevidence: The default SnapshotThreshold of 8192 keeps the replay range near the 8192-entry bound rather than far above it, so on a fully auto-snapshotting node the block needs the range to overshoot the bound, for example because more entries were appended between the snapshot trigger and the snapshot completion. The claim does not rest on the default configuration alone: SnapshotThreshold and MaxAppendEntries are both legal config fields, and a store that keeps its log without snapshots reaches any range.

The existing feature test (raft_test.go:1183-1270) restarts with a log of about a hundred entries, far below the bound, so its passing result is not counterevidence to a bound that begins around 8192 default entries.
limitations: The receipt for this question's fixed experiment is not yet part of this account; a native local run of the same harness was used only to validate the operands during construction and is not offered as evidence.

The harness restarts a single-voter in-memory cluster with SnapshotThreshold raised so that no automatic snapshot is taken; it does not exercise a lowered MaxAppendEntries, an overshooting auto-snapshot, or a multi-node member loss.

The blocked state is reported as non-return within a fixed window plus a stack sample of the blocked goroutine; the permanence argument comes from the source, since nothing consumes the channel before runFSM starts.

interpretations.rationale: Receipt 3d04552f58e548b0ae089192392b564f restarted two independently built single-voter prefixes whose retained store holds a committed log about 9000 entries above an absent snapshot: event 16 records 9000 applied commands, log_last_index 9002, staged_commit_index 9001, snapshot_index 0 and the resulting 141 replay batches at MaxAppendEntries 64, and event 19 records the same for the control prefix. Comparison 0 is violated by witness event 18: the restart admitted by event 17 (restore_committed_logs true) did not return from NewRaft within the 8000ms window (new_raft_returned false), and the sampled goroutine stack names the replay frames in order, processLogs at raft.go:1346 called from restoreFromCommittedLogs at api.go:753 called from NewRaft, which is the batch send on fsmMutateCh. Comparison 1 holds at event 21: the same prefix shape restarted with the flag off (admission event 20) returned from NewRaft in 1ms (new_raft_returned true, elapsed_ms 1) and then reached leadership (event 22, final_state Leader, commit_index 9003). The two restarts differ only in the flag, so the non-return is not a property of the prefix, the log volume or the transport. Source side, the mechanism is settled and makes the block permanent rather than slow: processLogs delivers each batch of at most MaxAppendEntries commit tuples through a select whose only other case is shutdownCh (raft.go:1302-1312), fsmMutateCh is created with capacity 128 (api.go:560), and its only consumer runFSM is started by api.go:636-638 after restoreFromCommittedLogs has returned. The replay needs ceil((commitIndex - lastApplied)/MaxAppendEntries) = ceil(9001/64) = 141 sends, so the 129th send waits for a consumer that cannot exist until the call it is blocking has finished, with no timeout, and the only escape is a shutdown channel that the caller cannot close because NewRaft has not returned the object. Scope of the defect statement: with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled, NewRaft cannot complete startup whenever the committed log it replays needs more than 128 batches, that is more than 128*MaxAppendEntries entries above the restored snapshot index; the bound is 8192 entries with the default MaxAppendEntries of 64, and is smaller in proportion to any smaller legal value. The failure is startup liveness, not a wrong decision: the node never begins participating at all, so a single-voter group stays down and a larger group permanently loses one member. The counterevidence is about how easily a default deployment reaches the bound, not about whether the block occurs once it is reached.

knowledge.assertion: Each batch is delivered with a select between a send on fsmMutateCh and shutdownCh, so a full channel with no consumer waits indefinitely.
fsmMutateCh has capacity 128 and its consumer runFSM starts only after the startup replay returns.
The number of entries replayed above the snapshot is what sets the batch count, and the automatic snapshot cadence is the only bound on that range in a default deployment.
With the flag on, lastApplied is set to the persisted commit index before the replay, so the replay range spans the committed log above the snapshot.

counterevidence: The evidence that NewRaft did not return is a single 8000ms window plus one stack sample (event 18). The claim that the wait is permanent does not rest on that sample: the source shows no timeout, exactly one consumer started after the blocked call returns, and an escape that requires an object the caller has not received. The flag-off control returning in 1ms (event 21) shows the wait is not simply the cost of the work.

With the default SnapshotThreshold of 8192 and MaxAppendEntries of 64, the automatic snapshot cadence keeps the replay range near the 8192-entry bound, so a default node blocks only when the range overshoots the bound, for example because entries kept arriving between the snapshot trigger and the snapshot completing. The harness therefore raised SnapshotThreshold, a legal Config field, to place the range unambiguously above the bound. The receipt establishes that crossing the bound blocks startup; it does not measure how often a default deployment crosses it.

The control's FSM catch-up was not observed to completion: event 22 samples last_applied 0 right after leadership, so the receipt shows only that the flag-off restart returns promptly and elects itself, not that its later catch-up finishes.

The blocked goroutine was abandoned inside the test process; the test completed because NewRaft ran in a separate goroutine. That is a harness choice, not a repair: the abandoned call still cannot be shut down, since the caller never received the object.
limitations: Both prefixes are single-voter in-memory clusters over an in-memory commit-tracking log store with SnapshotThreshold raised so no automatic snapshot moves the replay bound; the proportional relation for smaller MaxAppendEntries is source-derived (ceil(range/MaxAppendEntries) against a 128-slot buffer) and was not measured.
No multi-node cluster is exercised, so the member loss caused by a node that cannot start is argued rather than observed.
The bound itself depends on the caller-side store: the replay range comes from the store's persisted commit index, and the harness uses a test store whose staging is not atomic with its log writes.
Only one wait length (8000ms) was used, and the same case was not repeated; schedule variation is not characterized.

interpretations.rationale: Two executions of the same fixed experiment agree. Receipt e82594cc274340f0a961608cda519e00 first reruns the original pair: event 16 records a prefix with 9000 applied commands, log_last_index 9002, staged_commit_index 9001, snapshot_index 0 and 141 replay batches at MaxAppendEntries 64; the flag-on restart admitted by event 17 did not return from NewRaft within 8000ms (event 18, new_raft_returned false) and the sampled stack again names processLogs at raft.go:1346 called from restoreFromCommittedLogs at api.go:753 called from NewRaft, while the flag-off restart of the same shape returned in 5ms (event 21) and became leader (event 22). Receipt 3d04552f58e548b0ae089192392b564f recorded the same outcome with return in 1ms, so the block reproduces across two independent executions with different addresses. The revision then measures the bound: events 23 and 27 record two prefixes built the same way at MaxAppendEntries 16 with 1501 and 3001 replayed entries, that is 94 and 188 batches; the below-bound restart (comparison 0, event 25) returned from NewRaft in 0ms, and the above-bound restart (comparison 1, witness event 29) did not return, with the stack sample naming the same replay frames. Because the two cases share the flag, the batch size, the store machinery and the harness, and differ only in replay volume, the boundary between them measures the completion bound as 128 batches times MaxAppendEntries (2048 entries at 16, 8192 at the default 64) rather than a fixed amount of log. Source side, the mechanism is settled and makes the wait permanent rather than slow: processLogs delivers each batch through a select whose only other case is shutdownCh (raft.go:1302-1312), fsmMutateCh is created with capacity 128 (api.go:560), and its only consumer runFSM is started by api.go:636-638 after the replay returns; the replay needs ceil((commitIndex - lastApplied)/MaxAppendEntries) sends, so once the count passes 128 the 129th send waits for a consumer that cannot exist until the blocked call finishes, with no timeout and no reachable way to close shutdownCh because the caller never receives the object. Defect statement, now scoped to the measured bound: with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled, NewRaft cannot complete startup whenever the committed log it replays exceeds 128*MaxAppendEntries entries above the restored snapshot index; at the default MaxAppendEntries of 64 that is 8192 entries, and it is proportionally smaller for any smaller legal value, as measured at 16. The failure is startup liveness, not a wrong decision: the node never begins participating, so a single-voter group stays down and a larger group permanently loses one member.

The flag-off control returns in 1ms and 5ms across the two receipts (events 21 in each), so the wait is not the cost of the work.

The measured bound comes from one batch size: the below and above cases both ran at MaxAppendEntries 16, while the earlier pair shows blocking at 141 batches at MaxAppendEntries 64. No registration was run between 94 and 128 batches, so the exact boundary is bracketed rather than binary-searched, and the arithmetic form of the bound is still supported by the source rather than by the measurement alone.

With the default SnapshotThreshold of 8192 equal to the default bound, a default node blocks only when its committed range above the snapshot overshoots the bound; both the earlier and the revised cases raised SnapshotThreshold, a legal Config field, so how often a default deployment crosses the bound is not measured.

The below-bound restart returned from NewRaft but had not elected itself one second later (event 26: final_state Follower, leader_observed false, commit_index 1501). That is not a failure of this question's predicate, and it is also not explained by this receipt, which records no configuration operands; the sibling investigation's mechanism predicts an empty tracked configuration for exactly this restart, and that attribution is an open direction rather than an observation here.

The replay range comes from the caller-side store's persisted commit index, and the harness uses a test store whose staging is not atomic with its log writes, so the size of the range in a production deployment is a caller property that this receipt does not constrain.
limitations: Both prefixes are single-voter in-memory clusters over an in-memory commit-tracking log store, with SnapshotThreshold raised so no automatic snapshot moves the replay bound; no multi-node cluster is exercised, so the member loss caused by a node that cannot start is argued rather than observed.

The blocked NewRaft call is abandoned in a separate goroutine so the test can complete; that is a harness choice, not a repair, and it means the harness itself never observes the process-level consequence of a real startup hang.
Both executions use one wait length (8000ms) and one prefix shape per case; schedule variation beyond two runs is not characterized.
The bound is measured at two batch sizes (16 and 64) and one replay per side, so the claim is a measured threshold bracket plus a source-derived formula, not a scan of the boundary.
interpretations.joint_history: Both receipts belong to this investigation and are compatible as successive observations of the same prefix machinery: 3d04552f58e548b0ae089192392b564f is the predecessor fixed experiment, and e82594cc274340f0a961608cda519e00 is its revision, whose harness is a strict superset (the two original 9000-entry cases unchanged, plus the two MaxAppendEntries-16 cases). The original pair uses identical inputs in both harnesses and emits the same event names with the same operands apart from independently generated random addresses and observed return latencies, so the earlier receipt contributes reproducibility of the block and of the flag-off control, while the bound pair exists only in the later receipt.

interpretations.rationale: Recovery. Receipt 9a373c13725a42aa9f48f59c0f2f2f1c restarted four real single-voter prefixes on their retained stores with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs on and off. With the flag on and no snapshot, the node recovered an empty configuration (event 2: latest_config_index 0, no members, 268 polls with no leader) even though its log holds the bootstrap configuration entry at index 1 (event 0), while the flag-off control on the same prefix shape tracked that entry and elected itself in 17 polls (event 6); with a snapshot taken before a committed AddNonvoter, the flag-on node recovered the snapshot's index-1 configuration and never the log's committed index-7 configuration (events 10, 11), while the flag-off control recovered index 7 (event 15). Source side, the mechanism is settled: restoreFromCommittedLogs stores the persisted commit index and calls processLogs with it (api.go:723-754), which advances lastApplied before NewRaft runs the scan that rebuilds tracked configuration state from max(snapshotIndex, lastApplied)+1 (api.go:602-621); committed configuration entries at or below that bound are therefore never passed to processConfigurationLogEntry (raft.go:1605-1624), and the FSM's ConfigurationStore is not read back. The tracked configuration is what decides election eligibility (raft.go:225-246), quorum size (raft.go:1085-1094), the leader's commitment membership (raft.go:456-467, commitment.go:35-64) and the vote-admission checks. Consequence, now observed. Receipt 79a9cc34b3ce42e197c384775efecc3a builds three voters A, B and C (event 0), snapshots A while the committed configuration is still {A,B,C} (event 1, snapshot index 4), removes C so the committed configuration becomes {A,B} at log index 5 (event 2), then restarts A with the flag on while B is partitioned and C stays connected. A's tracked configuration is the snapshot's index-1 three-voter configuration and it contains C (event 3: latest_config_index 1, latest_config_voters 3, latest_config_ids including C, log_config_index 5, log_config_voters 2). A then won the election - counting C's vote, a server the committed configuration no longer contains - and, in event 4, applied the client command 'stale-quorum-entry' with apply_error null at index 10 term 4, advancing its commit index and applied index to 10, while B's log does not contain that index and C's log contains it at the same term 4. A's own match index alone cannot form a majority of three, and B had no transport path to A, so the second match the commitment counted can only have come from C: the entry was committed, applied to A's FSM and reported successful to the client by a quorum that is not a majority of the committed configuration {A,B}. Defect account for the whole question: with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled and a commit-tracking log store, NewRaft cannot roll the node's tracked membership configuration forward past max(snapshot index, persisted commit index), so a restarted node may keep an older or empty membership although its log already contains the committed configuration entries; the recovered node can then be permanently unable to participate (empty configuration), or, as observed here, decide leadership and commit index from a member set the committed configuration does not match, committing an entry that a real voter of the committed configuration does not hold. The failed predecessor execution of the multi-node experiment (receipt 4ed46b198c8d41618cc855df0a63d469, exit 1) is retained in the run's logs but is not cited as an execution of this interpretation: it stopped in the harness at the snapshot step with 'nothing new to snapshot' because the elected leader was not A and A had applied no entry, so it produced no comparison result about the target. The library's own test for the feature (raft_test.go:1183-1270) restarts with a snapshot whose configuration already equals the final configuration and asserts only the applied index, so it does not constrain this path.

98ee8dfd5fac4b84915f91ed4b094bcf-gap-1.explanation: Resolved by receipt 79a9cc34b3ce42e197c384775efecc3a. The stale recovered configuration changed two decisions observable outside the node: the election A won (event 4, a_became_leader true) counted C, a server the committed configuration had removed, towards the majority of its tracked three-voter configuration, and the commit that followed (event 4: entry index 10, term 4, apply_error null, a_commit_index 10, a_applied_index 10, a_fsm_applied_payload true) was decided while the committed configuration's other voter B, partitioned from A, did not hold the entry (b_log_has_entry false) and the removed server C did (c_log_has_entry true, c_entry_term 4). Because A's own match cannot form a majority of three and B had no transport path to A, the second match must have come from C, so the commit rule was applied against a member set that is not a majority of the committed configuration {A,B}.
