The violating scenario needs the removed server C to stay running and reachable after its removal, since its acknowledgement is what the stale majority counted. If an operator removes a server and also stops it, or if it is unreachable, the same stale configuration would instead leave A unable to commit, so the receipt shows the reachable-removed-server case rather than every case.

The harness chose A as the restarting leader and B as the partitioned node, and it moved leadership to A with the library's leadership transfer before the snapshot; those are setup choices. They do not supply the stale configuration (event 3 shows A tracking a configuration its log had already superseded) and they do not supply the acknowledgement (C's log holds the entry at the same term), but a different assignment of roles is not exercised.

The receipt shows that the leader committed and applied the entry and returned success to the caller, and that the committed configuration's other voter lacked it; it does not follow the entry to a later term to observe an actual loss from a state machine, so the demonstrated violation is of the commitment rule rather than a completed divergence.

The first execution of the multi-node experiment failed in the harness before any comparison (receipt 4ed46b198c8d41618cc855df0a63d469, exit 1, 'snapshot on A failed: nothing new to snapshot'), and its single parsed event carries no configuration operands; it is retained as a harness artifact and not as evidence about the target.

The removed server is kept running deliberately, and no message loss, reordering or crash of the leader is injected, so the observation is a decision defect under a clean transport rather than a fault-injection study.

interpretations.rationale: Mechanism. Block. Receipt 3d04552f58e548b0ae089192392b564f restarts a single-voter prefix holding 9001 committed entries above an absent snapshot (event 16, 141 batches at MaxAppendEntries 64); the flag-on restart admitted by event 17 did not return within 8000ms (event 18) with the stack naming processLogs at raft.go:1346 called from restoreFromCommittedLogs at api.go:753 called from NewRaft, while the flag-off restart of the same shape returned in 5ms (event 21) and became leader (event 22); receipt e82594cc274340f0a961608cda519e00 reproduces both with return in 1ms. The revision of that harness adds a flag-on pair at MaxAppendEntries 16: 1501 replayed entries, 94 batches, returned in 0ms (event 25, comparison holds); 3001 entries, 188 batches, did not return (event 29, comparison violated, stack naming the same frames). Same flag, same batch size, same stores, only the replay volume differs, so the boundary sits between 94 and 128 batches, that is at 128 * MaxAppendEntries entries - 2048 at 16 and 8192 at the default 64. Availability. Receipt ebb3bb9fa26547f790129eea909d1d5a builds three voters at MaxAppendEntries 16, commits 3000 commands through a leader that is not A (event 9: A's staged commit index 3000, snapshot index 0, 188 batches), and restarts A in a goroutine. With the flag on the call did not return within 8000ms and the stack sample again names the replay frames (event 10), while the group kept committing with two members live (event 11: commit_while_two_live_ok true); stopping the member that is neither the leader nor A then left a single live member and the next command failed with 'leadership lost while committing log' (event 11: commit_after_stop_ok false). With the flag off, the same prefix and the same stop left the pair {leader, A} live and the command succeeded (events 13, 14: new_raft_returned true in 0ms, commit_after_stop_ok true). The only difference between the two cases is whether the restarted member came back, so the lost commit is attributable to the member that never started. interpretations.rationale: Correction account, needed because the earlier interpretations of this question stated the reachable replay in replayed log entries. Source: processLogs appends a commit tuple only for entries prepareLog accepts - LogCommand and LogBarrier always, LogConfiguration only when protocolVersion > 2 - and none for LogNoop or the deprecated peer entries, and it flushes a batch when the batch reaches config.MaxAppendEntries (raft.go:1296-1364, prepareLog at raft.go:1364-1391). The delivered batch count is therefore ceil(tuples/MaxAppendEntries) for the tuples in the replayed range, and a count computed from the range's index span is an upper bound that can be loose when the range contains entries that produce no tuple. Corroboration from the retained boundary receipt 8a710c75d1814aafad5d24b536998539 (cited as non-supporting corroboration, since this account makes no defect judgment): the prefix whose replayed range ends at index 2049 spans 2049 entries but contains 2048 tuples, delivered as 128 batches (event 31), and NewRaft returned in 0ms (event 32); the prefix ending at 2050 contains 2049 tuples, delivered as 129 batches (event 34), and NewRaft did not return within 8000ms (event 35, three stack mentions naming the replay frames). The entry-based figure the harness computes for the returning case also reads 129 batches, which is exactly the overstatement the correction describes. What does not change: the mechanism (a full 128-slot channel whose only consumer starts after the replay returns, with no timeout), the fact that the replay is bounded by the committed range above the restored snapshot, and the consequences already recorded, since command-dominated logs deliver close to one tuple per entry. What changes: the exact threshold should be stated in delivered batches - 128 * MaxAppendEntries tuples, 8192 at the default MaxAppendEntries of 64 - and a bound stated in log entries is an upper bound rather than an equality, with the gap widening on logs that carry no-op entries or, below protocol version 3, configuration entries.

3bdf46ca8b274b719cc26e672b951e75-gap-2.explanation: The corrected unit is commit tuples. prepareLog decides it: commands and barriers always produce a tuple, configuration entries only above protocol version 2, and no-op and deprecated peer entries never do (raft.go:1364-1391), while processLogs flushes a batch when the accumulated tuples reach MaxAppendEntries (raft.go:1336-1350). So the number of sends is ceil(tuples/MaxAppendEntries), and any figure derived from a log index range is an upper bound on that number.

3bdf46ca8b274b719cc26e672b951e75-gap-3.explanation: The retained boundary receipt shows the correction in an observation rather than only in the source: a replayed range of 2049 entries ending at index 2049 held 2048 tuples and was delivered as 128 batches, and NewRaft returned in 0ms (events 31, 32), while the range ending at 2050 held 2049 tuples and 129 batches and did not return (events 34, 35). The entry-based count the harness computes reads 129 in the returning case as well, which is the overstatement the correction names.

3bdf46ca8b274b719cc26e672b951e75-gap-4.explanation: For the earlier interpretations, the change is one of precision rather than of substance: their threshold expressions in replayed entries remain upper bounds, valid where the replayed range is dominated by commands and configuration entries at protocol 3 or above, and the mechanism, the 128-slot channel, the observable block and its consequences are unaffected. The successor account for this question states the bound in delivered batches and cites the batching behaviour at revision 2, so the recorded conclusion no longer rests on the entry-based phrasing.

The correction widens in the other direction too: below protocol version 3 the replayed range can contain many configuration entries that produce no tuple, so an entry-based threshold can overstate the reachable batch count by far more than the one or two entries seen at protocol 3, while the mechanism and its consequences are unchanged.
This account makes no defect judgment of its own; the defect account for this question remains the experiment-cited interpretation, whose conclusion is unaffected by the counting unit.

interpretations.rationale: Correction note: this successor differs from the previous account of this question only by a transcribed latency; the control's election is now stated as the receipt records it (19 polls at a 5ms interval, about 95ms), not from an earlier construction run. Everything else - sources, executions, knowledge uses, counterevidence and limitations - is unchanged. Recovery. Receipt 9a373c13725a42aa9f48f59c0f2f2f1c restarted four real single-voter prefixes on their retained stores with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs on and off: with the flag on and no snapshot the node recovered an empty configuration (event 2: no members at index 0, 268 polls without a leader) although its log holds the bootstrap configuration entry at index 1 (event 0), the flag-off control on the same prefix shape tracked that entry and elected itself (event 6), and with a snapshot taken before a committed AddNonvoter the flag-on node kept the snapshot's index-1 configuration instead of the log's committed index-7 configuration (events 10, 11) while the flag-off control recovered index 7 (event 15). Source side the mechanism is settled: restoreFromCommittedLogs stores the persisted commit index and calls processLogs with it (api.go:723-754), advancing lastApplied before NewRaft runs the scan that rebuilds tracked configuration state from max(snapshotIndex, lastApplied)+1 (api.go:602-621), so committed configuration entries at or below that bound never reach processConfigurationLogEntry (raft.go:1605-1624) and the FSM's ConfigurationStore is never read back. That state decides election eligibility (raft.go:225-246), quorum size (raft.go:1085-1094), the leader's commitment membership (raft.go:456-467, commitment.go:35-64) and vote admission. First consequence: receipt 79a9cc34b3ce42e197c384775efecc3a removed server C from {A,B,C} (event 2: committed configuration at index 5 with two voters), restarted A with the flag on while B was partitioned, and A tracked the snapshot's index-1 three-voter configuration containing C (event 3); A won the election counting C and committed 'stale-quorum-entry' at index 10 term 4 with apply_error null, its FSM applied it, B's log lacked that index and C's log held it at the same term (event 4). Since A's own match cannot form a majority of three and B had no transport path, the deciding acknowledgement can only have come from C: the entry was committed, applied and reported successful against a member set that is not a majority of the committed configuration. Second consequence, durable: receipt c477da09810f4842ba55130320e2a6b5 leaves A in that recovered state on a three-voter cluster (event 6: latest_config_index 0 with no members and committed_config_index 0, against its log's index-1 three-voter entry and staged commit index 4), takes a snapshot through the library's normal path, and reads back metadata recording no configuration at index 0 while the log establishes a three-voter configuration at index 1 (event 7, snapshot_config_matches_log_config false). A then restarts on the same stores with the replay disabled and comes up with an empty configuration at index 0, no leader within 1500ms, in state Follower (event 8). The loss is therefore not confined to the replay path: once written, the snapshot metadata re-imposes it on a restart that never enables the feature. Defect account: with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled and a commit-tracking log store, NewRaft cannot roll the node's tracked membership configuration forward past max(snapshot index, persisted commit index), so the node may keep an older or empty membership although its own log already contains the committed configuration entries; the recovered node can be permanently unable to participate, can decide leadership and commit index from a member set the committed configuration does not match - committing an entry a real voter of that configuration does not hold - and can write the lost configuration into durable snapshot metadata, from which later restarts, including ones with the feature disabled, restore it. The library's own test for the feature (raft_test.go:1183-1270) restarts with a snapshot whose configuration already equals the final configuration and asserts only the applied index, so it does not constrain this path. The failed first execution of the multi-node experiment (receipt 4ed46b198c8d41618cc855df0a63d469, exit 1) is retained in the run's logs but is not cited as an execution here: it stopped in the harness at the snapshot step because the elected leader was not the node being snapshotted, so it produced no comparison result about the target.

knowledge.assertion: The startup configuration scan runs from max(lastSnapshotIndex, lastApplied)+1, so entries at or below that bound never reach processConfigurationLogEntry at startup.
restoreFromCommittedLogs stores the store's commit index and calls processLogs with it only when the flag is set, which advances lastApplied to that index before the scan runs.
processConfigurationLogEntry is the only writer of the tracked configuration state; FSM-side configuration storage does not feed back into it.
The tracked latest configuration feeds quorumSize, the leader's commitment membership, leader-lease voter counting and the vote-admission checks.
A follower with configurations.latestIndex equal to 0 does not start an election, which is terminal when no reachable peer can supply a configuration entry.
Snapshots record the committed configuration and its index that the node currently tracks, and startup restores that metadata into the tracked configuration.

counterevidence: The doc comment for RestoreCommittedLogs (config.go:243-254) promises only that committed logs are replayed to catch the FSM up and says nothing about membership recovery, so the stale tracked configuration can be read as an unnamed side effect of a feature that never claimed to preserve it. The counter is that the startup scan at api.go:610-621 exists to rebuild that state from the log, and the observed consequences are a commit decided against a member set the committed configuration does not contain and a durable record that re-imposes the loss.

The commit-rule violation needs the removed server C to stay reachable after its removal, since its acknowledgement is what the stale majority counted; if it were stopped or unreachable the same stale configuration would instead leave the node unable to commit. The receipt therefore shows one reachable-removed-server case rather than every case.

One could argue the snapshot in the durable-state case is only as good as the state the node tracks, and that a caller should not snapshot a node whose configuration is empty. The counter is that the node is an ordinary cluster member whose own log contains the configuration entries, nothing in the API or the documentation marks its snapshots as unusable, and the resulting metadata then defeats a restart that has the feature disabled, so the corruption outlives the condition that created it.

The flag-off restart's failure to lead could be attributed to the 1500ms observation window rather than to the empty configuration. The counter is the source guard that refuses elections while configurations.latestIndex is zero (raft.go:225-241), together with the control on the same prefix shape that elected itself in 19 polls of the harness's 5ms interval, about 95ms (receipt 9a373c13725a42aa9f48f59c0f2f2f1c, event 6 records polls 19 and leader_observed true); 1500ms is 30 election timeouts.

The harness assigns roles deliberately (A restarts, B is partitioned, leadership is moved with the library's transfer) and it takes the snapshot explicitly rather than through the automatic cadence. Those choices select the scenario but do not supply the stale or empty configuration, which event 6 shows against the node's own log, nor the acknowledgement, which C's log carries.

The first execution of the multi-node experiment failed in the harness before any comparison (receipt 4ed46b198c8d41618cc855df0a63d469) and is retained as a harness artifact; the later receipts contain the same scenario with both defects exercised.
limitations: All nodes are in-memory transports and stores in one process and the harness uses a test log store whose staging is not atomic with its log writes; the caller-side durability contract of CommitTrackingLogStore is assumed, not verified, and no production store or snapshot store is exercised.

The durable-state case snapshots a node that has no snapshot on its stores and then restarts with the replay disabled; shipping such a snapshot to a follower, or corruption arising from the automatic snapshot cadence, is not exercised, and deleting the corrupt snapshot is not tested as a recovery.

The multi-node case is one prefix shape with one committed removal, keeps the removed server running, and injects no message loss, reordering or crash, so the decision defect is observed under a clean transport.

Schedule variation is limited: the multi-node scenario appears in two receipts with the same operands, the durable-state scenario in one, and the observation windows are 1500ms for non-participation and 2000ms apply timeouts.
interpretations.joint_history: All three receipts are executions of this investigation's fixed experiments on the same captured source revision, in separate workspaces with no shared mutable state. Receipt 9a373c13725a42aa9f48f59c0f2f2f1c established the recovery behaviour on four single-voter prefixes; receipt 79a9cc34b3ce42e197c384775efecc3a exercised the same recovery as the setup of a three-voter cluster and observed the commit-rule consequence; receipt c477da09810f4842ba55130320e2a6b5 contains both that three-voter scenario again (events 0-4, with the same operands: a restart tracking the snapshot's index-1 three-voter configuration against a log whose newest configuration entry is index 4 with two voters, and a commit at index 9 completed with only the removed server's acknowledgement) and the new durable-state scenario (events 5-8, where the same recovery leaves an empty tracked configuration). The repeated scenario reproduces the earlier witness with fresh addresses, so the premises each receipt relies on are observed more than once and the newer receipts only add consequences.

interpretations.rationale: Correction note: this successor differs from the previous account of this question only in two transcribed numbers and their attribution; the flag-off control of receipt 3d04552f58e548b0ae089192392b564f returned in 1ms and the same control of receipt e82594cc274340f0a961608cda519e00 returned in 5ms, as those receipts record, and the earlier account had them swapped. Everything else - sources, executions, knowledge uses, counterevidence, limitations and joint history - is unchanged. Mechanism. With Config.RestoreCommittedLogs set, NewRaft reads the persisted commit index and calls processLogs with it before starting any background goroutine (api.go:723-754). processLogs walks the committed range and appends a commit tuple only for entries prepareLog accepts - commands and barriers always, configuration entries when protocolVersion > 2, and nothing for no-op or deprecated peer entries - flushing a batch whenever the batch reaches config.MaxAppendEntries and delivering it through a select whose only other case is shutdownCh (raft.go:1296-1364 with prepareLog at raft.go:1364-1391). fsmMutateCh is created with capacity 128 (api.go:560) and its only consumer runFSM is started by api.go:636-638 after the replay returns, so a replay needing more than 128 delivered batches waits for a consumer that cannot exist until the blocked call finishes, with no timeout. Block and bound. Receipt 3d04552f58e548b0ae089192392b564f restarts a single-voter prefix holding 9001 committed entries above an absent snapshot (event 16, 141 delivered batches at MaxAppendEntries 64); the flag-on restart admitted by event 17 did not return within 8000ms (event 18, stack naming processLogs at raft.go:1346 called from restoreFromCommittedLogs at api.go:753 called from NewRaft) while the flag-off restart of the same shape returned in 1ms (event 21) and became leader (event 22); receipt e82594cc274340f0a961608cda519e00 reproduces both, with its own flag-off control returning in 5ms (its event 21) and adds a pair at MaxAppendEntries 16 where 1501 replayed entries (94 batches) returned in 0ms (event 25) and 3001 entries (188 batches) did not (event 29). Receipt 8a710c75d1814aafad5d24b536998539 then places the boundary exactly: at MaxAppendEntries 16 one prefix ends at staged commit index 2049, whose replayed range contains 2048 entries that become commit tuples, that is 128 delivered batches (event 31), and NewRaft returned in 0ms (event 32, comparison holds); the other ends at 2050 with 2049 tuples, that is 129 delivered batches (event 34), and NewRaft did not return within 8000ms (event 35, comparison violated, three stack mentions naming the replay frames). The pair differs only in one replayed command, so the bound is the 128-slot channel measured in delivered batches, and any count derived from the log's index range is an upper bound: the entry-based figure for the returning case also reads 129 batches (event 31), because the range includes entries that produce no tuple. Availability. Receipt ebb3bb9fa26547f790129eea909d1d5a builds three voters at MaxAppendEntries 16, commits 3000 commands through a leader that is not A (event 9), restarts A in a goroutine, and observes the same non-return (event 10). With the replay on the group kept committing with two members live and lost the ability after one further member was stopped (event 11: commit_while_two_live_ok true, commit_after_stop_ok false, error 'leadership lost while committing log'), while with the replay off the same stop left the pair {leader, A} live and the command succeeded (events 13, 14). The corrected unit matters for the recorded gaps: the three correction gaps ask about the premise change, and the receipt answers them substantively - the returning case's entry-based figure was 129 batches while only 128 were delivered, so counts derived from a log index range are upper bounds. Defect account: with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled, NewRaft cannot complete startup whenever the replay delivers more than 128 batches, that is more than 128*MaxAppendEntries entries that become commit tuples above the restored snapshot index; at the default MaxAppendEntries of 64 that is 8192 tuples, and it is proportionally smaller for any smaller legal value, as measured at 16 (2048 tuples returning, 2049 blocking). The failure is a startup liveness failure: the node never begins participating, so a single-voter group stays down, a larger group runs with proportionally less fault tolerance, and one further stop was enough to make a three-voter group unable to commit. Pending operations the leader had accepted are answered with ErrLeadershipLost once it steps down (raft.go:508-528).

knowledge.assertion: Batches are counted in commit tuples, so no-op and deprecated peer entries consume no batch slot and configuration entries do so only above protocol version 2.
fsmMutateCh has capacity 128 and its consumer runFSM starts only after the startup replay returns.
The replay range above the snapshot sets the number of tuples to deliver, and the automatic snapshot cadence is the only bound on that range in a default deployment.
With the flag on, lastApplied is set to the persisted commit index before the replay, so the replay range spans the committed log above the snapshot.
The tracked latest configuration feeds quorumSize and the vote-admission checks, which is why a member that never starts is simply absent from every future majority.

counterevidence: The block itself is evidenced by non-return within an 8000ms window plus a stack sample per blocked case (events 18, 29, 10 and 35). The permanence argument does not rest on those samples: the source shows no timeout, a single consumer started only after the blocked call returns, and an escape requiring an object the caller has not received. The flag-off controls return promptly in each receipt: 1ms at event 21 of receipt 3d04552f58e548b0ae089192392b564f, 5ms at event 21 and 0ms at event 25 of receipt e82594cc274340f0a961608cda519e00, and 0ms at event 13 of receipt ebb3bb9fa26547f790129eea909d1d5a.

The boundary pair is a single run per side, and its delivered-tuple count is computed by the harness scanning the replayed range with the same type rule prepareLog uses rather than read from an internal counter; the behaviour itself straddles the boundary by one replayed command, and the tuple figure is an inspectable operand rather than the decisive predicate.

With the default SnapshotThreshold of 8192 equal to the default bound in tuples, a default node blocks only when the committed range above its newest snapshot exceeds 8192 tuple-producing entries; every case here raised SnapshotThreshold, a legal Config field, so how readily a default deployment crosses the bound is not measured.

The availability case contains a deliberate second stop, so what it shows is the loss of the group's fault-tolerance margin rather than an outage in an untouched cluster; the control with the replay disabled performs the same stop and still commits, which is what attributes the loss to the member that did not return.

In the flag-on availability case the surviving leader's command failed with 'leadership lost while committing log', which is the leader stepping down and failing its pending operations rather than a defect of its own; the same apply succeeded while two members were live (event 11) and after the same stop in the control (event 14).

The blocked NewRaft call is abandoned in a separate goroutine so the tests can complete; that is a harness choice, not a repair, and no harness observes the process-level consequence of a caller that waits forever.
limitations: All cases run in one process over in-memory transports and a test commit-tracking store; no production store, no process-level restart and no disk fault are exercised, and the confined goroutine is the only trace of the real caller's hang.

The availability case uses one prefix shape, one batch size (16) and one extra stop; the boundary case uses one batch size and one run per side; observation windows are 8000ms for restarts and 3000ms for the applies.
Schedule variation is limited: the original pair appears in two receipts, the bound pair, the boundary pair and the availability pair in one each, and each blocked state is sampled once.
The bound's dependence on the caller-side store is assumed rather than verified: the replay range comes from the stored commit index, whose durability contract belongs to the LogStore implementation.

Receipt 3d04552f58e548b0ae089192392b564f restarts a single-voter prefix holding 9001 committed entries above an absent snapshot (event 16, 141 delivered batches at MaxAppendEntries 64); the flag-on restart admitted by event 17 did not return within 8000ms (event 18, stack naming processLogs at raft.go:1346 called from restoreFromCommittedLogs at api.go:753 called from NewRaft) while the flag-off restart of the same shape returned in 1ms (event 21) and became leader (event 22); receipt e82594cc274340f0a961608cda519e00 reproduces both, with its own flag-off control returning in 5ms (its event 21) and adds a pair at MaxAppendEntries 16 where 1501 replayed entries (94 batches) returned in 0ms (event 25) and 3001 entries (188 batches) did not (event 29). interpretations.rationale: Extension note: this successor adds receipt 4178d9d5c479470cafb7ebd7951a9332, which observes in a three-voter group that a node recovering without a configuration never attempts candidacy while the same node and log with the replay disabled do; the sources, the three earlier executions, the knowledge uses, the conclusion and the remaining counterevidence are otherwise unchanged, and the counter about the observation window is strengthened with the new control's sample counts. Correction note: this successor differs from the previous account of this question only by a transcribed latency; the control's election is now stated as the receipt records it (19 polls at a 5ms interval, about 95ms), not from an earlier construction run. Everything else - sources, executions, knowledge uses, counterevidence and limitations - is unchanged. Recovery. Receipt 9a373c13725a42aa9f48f59c0f2f2f1c restarted four real single-voter prefixes on their retained stores with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs on and off: with the flag on and no snapshot the node recovered an empty configuration (event 2: no members at index 0, 268 polls without a leader) although its log holds the bootstrap configuration entry at index 1 (event 0), the flag-off control on the same prefix shape tracked that entry and elected itself (event 6), and with a snapshot taken before a committed AddNonvoter the flag-on node kept the snapshot's index-1 configuration instead of the log's committed index-7 configuration (events 10, 11) while the flag-off control recovered index 7 (event 15). Source side the mechanism is settled: restoreFromCommittedLogs stores the persisted commit index and calls processLogs with it (api.go:723-754), advancing lastApplied before NewRaft runs the scan that rebuilds tracked configuration state from max(snapshotIndex, lastApplied)+1 (api.go:602-621), so committed configuration entries at or below that bound never reach processConfigurationLogEntry (raft.go:1605-1624) and the FSM's ConfigurationStore is never read back. That state decides election eligibility (raft.go:225-246), quorum size (raft.go:1085-1094), the leader's commitment membership (raft.go:456-467, commitment.go:35-64) and vote admission. First consequence: receipt 79a9cc34b3ce42e197c384775efecc3a removed server C from {A,B,C} (event 2: committed configuration at index 5 with two voters), restarted A with the flag on while B was partitioned, and A tracked the snapshot's index-1 three-voter configuration containing C (event 3); A won the election counting C and committed 'stale-quorum-entry' at index 10 term 4 with apply_error null, its FSM applied it, B's log lacked that index and C's log held it at the same term (event 4). Since A's own match cannot form a majority of three and B had no transport path, the deciding acknowledgement can only have come from C: the entry was committed, applied and reported successful against a member set that is not a majority of the committed configuration. Authority attempt. Receipt 4178d9d5c479470cafb7ebd7951a9332 builds a three-voter group, commits three commands so the staged commit index is non-zero, restarts A over its own stores and reads its tracked configuration: with the replay enabled A tracks no configuration at all (event 15: latest_config_index 0, no members, staged commit index 4), and in 266 samples over 1500ms of hearing no leader with the other voters shut down it was a follower in every sample and never a candidate (event 16, comparison violated); with the replay disabled the same node and the same log recover the three-voter configuration (event 17: latest_config_index 1, three members) and the node was a candidate in 254 of 266 samples, ending in state Candidate (event 18, comparison holds). A node whose tracked configuration is empty therefore does not merely fail to win an election: it never attempts to acquire authority, so it cannot be the source of a new leader even when the surviving members could form a quorum with it. Second consequence, durable: receipt c477da09810f4842ba55130320e2a6b5 leaves A in that recovered state on a three-voter cluster (event 6: latest_config_index 0 with no members and committed_config_index 0, against its log's index-1 three-voter entry and staged commit index 4), takes a snapshot through the library's normal path, and reads back metadata recording no configuration at index 0 while the log establishes a three-voter configuration at index 1 (event 7, snapshot_config_matches_log_config false). A then restarts on the same stores with the replay disabled and comes up with an empty configuration at index 0, no leader within 1500ms, in state Follower (event 8). The loss is therefore not confined to the replay path: once written, the snapshot metadata re-imposes it on a restart that never enables the feature. Defect account: with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled and a commit-tracking log store, NewRaft cannot roll the node's tracked membership configuration forward past max(snapshot index, persisted commit index), so the node may keep an older or empty membership although its own log already contains the committed configuration entries; the recovered node can be permanently unable to participate, can decide leadership and commit index from a member set the committed configuration does not match - committing an entry a real voter of that configuration does not hold - and can write the lost configuration into durable snapshot metadata, from which later restarts, including ones with the feature disabled, restore it. The library's own test for the feature (raft_test.go:1183-1270) restarts with a snapshot whose configuration already equals the final configuration and asserts only the applied index, so it does not constrain this path. The failed first execution of the multi-node experiment (receipt 4ed46b198c8d41618cc855df0a63d469, exit 1) is retained in the run's logs but is not cited as an execution here: it stopped in the harness at the snapshot step because the elected leader was not the node being snapshotted, so it produced no comparison result about the target.

knowledge.assertion: The startup configuration scan runs from max(lastSnapshotIndex, lastApplied)+1, so entries at or below that bound never reach processConfigurationLogEntry at startup.
restoreFromCommittedLogs stores the store's commit index and calls processLogs with it only when the flag is set, which advances lastApplied to that index before the scan runs.
processConfigurationLogEntry is the only writer of the tracked configuration state; FSM-side configuration storage does not feed back into it.
The tracked latest configuration feeds quorumSize, the leader's commitment membership, leader-lease voter counting and the vote-admission checks.
A follower with configurations.latestIndex equal to 0 does not start an election, which is terminal when no reachable peer can supply a configuration entry.
Snapshots record the committed configuration and its index that the node currently tracks, and startup restores that metadata into the tracked configuration.

counterevidence: The doc comment for RestoreCommittedLogs (config.go:243-254) promises only that committed logs are replayed to catch the FSM up and says nothing about membership recovery, so the stale tracked configuration can be read as an unnamed side effect of a feature that never claimed to preserve it. The counter is that the startup scan at api.go:610-621 exists to rebuild that state from the log, and the observed consequences are a commit decided against a member set the committed configuration does not contain and a durable record that re-imposes the loss.

The commit-rule violation needs the removed server C to stay reachable after its removal, since its acknowledgement is what the stale majority counted; if it were stopped or unreachable the same stale configuration would instead leave the node unable to commit. The receipt therefore shows one reachable-removed-server case rather than every case.

One could argue the snapshot in the durable-state case is only as good as the state the node tracks, and that a caller should not snapshot a node whose configuration is empty. The counter is that the node is an ordinary cluster member whose own log contains the configuration entries, nothing in the API or the documentation marks its snapshots as unusable, and the resulting metadata then defeats a restart that has the feature disabled, so the corruption outlives the condition that created it.

The flag-off restart's failure to lead could be attributed to the 1500ms observation window rather than to the empty configuration. The counter is the source guard that refuses elections while configurations.latestIndex is zero (raft.go:225-241) plus two controls inside the same window: the single-voter control elected itself in 19 polls of the harness's 5ms interval (receipt 9a373c13725a42aa9f48f59c0f2f2f1c, event 6), and in the authority case the node that recovered its configuration was a candidate in 254 of 266 samples while the node with the empty configuration showed zero candidate samples (receipt 4178d9d5c479470cafb7ebd7951a9332, events 16 and 18).

The harness assigns roles deliberately (A restarts, B is partitioned, leadership is moved with the library's transfer) and it takes the snapshot explicitly rather than through the automatic cadence. Those choices select the scenario but do not supply the stale or empty configuration, which event 6 shows against the node's own log, nor the acknowledgement, which C's log carries.

The first execution of the multi-node experiment failed in the harness before any comparison (receipt 4ed46b198c8d41618cc855df0a63d469) and is retained as a harness artifact; the later receipts contain the same scenario with both defects exercised.

The authority case removes the other voters by shutting them down, so it shows that the defective node never attempts candidacy; it does not show an outage that a correct recovery would have prevented, because the recovered three-voter configuration also lacks a quorum with one voter left. What the receipt adds is the capability difference, not a counterfactual outage.
limitations: All nodes are in-memory transports and stores in one process and the harness uses a test log store whose staging is not atomic with its log writes; the caller-side durability contract of CommitTrackingLogStore is assumed, not verified, and no production store or snapshot store is exercised.

The durable-state case snapshots a node that has no snapshot on its stores and then restarts with the replay disabled; shipping such a snapshot to a follower, or corruption arising from the automatic snapshot cadence, is not exercised, and deleting the corrupt snapshot is not tested as a recovery.

The multi-node case is one prefix shape with one committed removal, keeps the removed server running, and injects no message loss, reordering or crash, so the decision defect is observed under a clean transport.

Schedule variation is limited: the multi-node scenario appears in two receipts with the same operands, the durable-state scenario in one, and the observation windows are 1500ms for non-participation and 2000ms apply timeouts.

limitations: All cases run in one process over in-memory transports and a test commit-tracking store; no production store, no process-level restart and no disk fault are exercised, and the confined goroutine is the only trace of the real caller's hang.

The availability case uses one prefix shape, one batch size (16) and one extra stop; the boundary case uses one batch size and one run per side; observation windows are 8000ms for restarts and 3000ms for the applies.

Schedule variation is unevenly covered: the original 9000-entry pair appears in two receipts, the boundary pair and the default-configuration pair have each been executed twice from the same fixed inputs with identical operands, while the bound pair and the availability pair remain single-run, and each blocked state is still sampled once per execution.
The bound's dependence on the caller-side store is assumed rather than verified: the replay range comes from the stored commit index, whose durability contract belongs to the LogStore implementation.
interpretations.joint_history: All four receipts are executions of fixed experiments for this investigation on the same captured source revision, in separate workspaces with no shared mutable state, and their harnesses share the same initialization: an in-memory commit-tracking log store, a single-voter bootstrap for the first three, RestoreCommittedLogs enabled on the prefix, and the restart in a separate goroutine with an 8000ms window. result.summary: Reported the repeat of the multi-node experiment honestly and submitted a revised authority experiment. Receipt fe822d82c6264158826e0303b4ce59b1 reproduced the commit-rule case (events 2-4: snapshot-era three-voter configuration against a log whose configuration entry has two voters, commit at index 10 with only the removed server's acknowledgement), the durable-snapshot case (events 6-8: empty configuration at index 0 in the snapshot metadata, empty after a flag-off restart) and the availability case (events 11, 13) with identical operands, but did not reproduce the authority witness: A's persisted commit index was 0 in that execution, so restoreFromCommittedLogs left lastApplied at zero, the scan started at index 1, A recovered the three-voter configuration (event 15) and did attempt candidacy with 255 of 267 samples in Candidate (event 16), which is why the comparison returned unknown. scope.description: Restart a single-voter raft node on top of its own retained stores, once with RestoreCommittedLogs enabled and once with it disabled, on two prefix shapes: a prefix with no snapshot, and a prefix whose snapshot precedes a committed configuration change. Report the recovered configuration (index, membership) beside the newest configuration entry in the node's own log, and whether the restarted node reaches leadership inside a 1.5s window (30 election/heartbeat timeouts at 50ms).
assumptions: The prefix runs with RestoreCommittedLogs enabled so that the commit index is staged into the commit-tracking log store; otherwise a restart with the feature enabled reads 0 and the scan start would equal the snapshot index.
The restarted node keeps the same address and ID as the prefix, so the configuration recorded in its log and snapshot still refers to it.

The FSM is an in-memory MockFSM and a fresh instance is used for each restart, which is the mode the feature targets; the FSM state is therefore rebuilt from the snapshot plus the replayed committed logs.

InmemCommitTrackingStore is a test facility whose StageCommitIndex does not share a write with StoreLogs; the probe uses it only as the store that exposes a persisted commit index and does not claim its durability properties.
excluded: No multi-node cluster, partition, or crash of a leader is exercised, so the commit-loss consequence of a stale member set is not measured here.
No snapshot-on-start or FSM-implemented ConfigurationStore variant is exercised.
No production log store (for example a bolt-backed store) is exercised; the caller-side durability contract of CommitTrackingLogStore is assumed, not verified.

basis.prefix: Each case calls assuranceBuildPrefix: NewInmemTransport with a fresh random address; inmemConfig with LocalID = 'server-' + address and RestoreCommittedLogs = true; NewInmemCommitTrackingStore, NewInmemStore and NewInmemSnapshotStore; BootstrapCluster with a single Voter server at that address; NewRaft with a fresh MockFSM. The prefix then waits for real leadership through the normal election path, applies four LogCommand entries, and for the snapshot cases takes a real Snapshot, then issues AddNonvoter for a peer that never connects (committed by the single voter) and applies two more commands. GetCommitIndex, LastIndex and a per-index log scan record the persisted commit index and every configuration entry with its index and membership, then Shutdown closes the node. The case then creates a new transport bound to the same address, copies the config with RestoreCommittedLogs set to the case value, and calls NewRaft with the same log store, stable store, snapshot store and a fresh MockFSM. It polls State() every 5ms for 1500ms, then asks the main thread for the tracked configurations through r.configurationsCh (the same channel takeSnapshot uses) and reads snapshot index, AppliedIndex, CommitIndex and LastIndex.
basis.responsibility: raft's NewRaft is responsible for re-establishing the node's membership configuration from the node's own durable state before any election or quorum decision is made; the caller is responsible for supplying a log store whose GetCommitIndex is atomic with StoreLogs and for enabling RestoreCommittedLogs deliberately.

comparisons.description: A node restarted with RestoreCommittedLogs on top of stores whose log holds a committed configuration entry must still be able to elect a leader inside the observation window.
Control: the same prefix shape restarted with RestoreCommittedLogs off reaches leadership, which shows the nonprogress is specific to the replay path and not to the prefix.
The configuration recovered at startup must equal the newest configuration entry in the node's own log (index and voter/nonvoter membership).
Control: with the feature off the same predicate holds on the same prefix shape.
After restarting on a snapshot that predates a committed configuration change, the recovered configuration must include that committed entry.
Control: the same snapshot-plus-configuration prefix restarted with the feature off does recover the committed configuration entry.

scope.description: Build single-voter prefixes whose committed log lies about 9000 entries above an absent snapshot, then restart each prefix with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs on and off, calling NewRaft in a goroutine and reporting whether it returned within 8000ms together with a stack sample of the blocked goroutine.
assumptions: The prefix runs with RestoreCommittedLogs enabled and a raised SnapshotThreshold so the commit index is staged into the commit-tracking log store and no automatic snapshot moves the replay bound.
The restarted node keeps the same address and ID as its prefix and uses a fresh in-memory MockFSM, so the whole committed log above the snapshot is replayed.
The observation window of 8000ms is used only to decide completion; the claim that the block persists comes from the source, since the channel's consumer is started only after the replay returns.
excluded: No lowered MaxAppendEntries case, so the proportional relation between the bound and MaxAppendEntries is source-derived and not measured.
No multi-node cluster, so member loss caused by a node that cannot start is not measured.
No production log store, and no store whose StageCommitIndex is atomic with StoreLogs.

basis.prefix: For each case, the harness builds its own prefix: NewInmemTransport with a random address, inmemConfig with LocalID = 'server-' + address, RestoreCommittedLogs true, SnapshotThreshold 1<<30 and SnapshotInterval one hour, plus NewInmemCommitTrackingStore, NewInmemStore and NewInmemSnapshotStore; BootstrapCluster with one Voter; NewRaft with a fresh MockFSM; wait for real leadership; then 9000 Apply calls, each waiting for its future. It records the store's commit index, last index, snapshot index and the computed batch count, then Shutdown. The case creates a new transport on the same address, copies the config with RestoreCommittedLogs set to the case value, and calls NewRaft in a separate goroutine. The main goroutine waits up to 8000ms for that call to return; if it does not, it samples all goroutine stacks with runtime.Stack and reports the excerpt around the first frame naming restoreFromCommittedLogs. If NewRaft returns, the harness waits up to one second for leadership, reports the state and then shuts the node down.
basis.responsibility: NewRaft owns completion of its own startup work, including the RestoreCommittedLogs replay it performs before returning; the caller cannot observe or interrupt a NewRaft call that has not returned, so any unbounded wait in that path is owned by the library.

comparisons.description: NewRaft must return for a node whose stores hold a committed log; a restart that replays more than the FSM channel can hold must not leave NewRaft waiting forever.
Control: the same prefix shape restarted with the replay disabled returns from NewRaft, which distinguishes the replay path from a property of the prefix.

scope.description: Restart single-voter prefixes with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled and Config.MaxAppendEntries 16, once with a committed log of about 1500 entries (94 replay batches, below the 128-slot capacity) and once with about 3000 entries (188 batches, above it), calling NewRaft in a goroutine and reporting whether it returned within 8000ms plus a stack sample of the blocked goroutine. The same harness also reruns the two 9000-entry default-batch cases of the predecessor so the earlier observations stay in one artifact.
assumptions: MaxAppendEntries 16 is a legal configuration (ValidateConfig only requires a positive value) and is applied to both the prefix and the restart, so the batch size is the same on both sides of the comparison.
SnapshotThreshold is raised so no automatic snapshot moves the replay range, and the prefix runs with the feature enabled so the commit index is staged into the commit-tracking log store.
The 8000ms window decides completion only; the permanence of a block comes from the source, since the channel's consumer starts only after the blocked call returns.
excluded: No production log store, no multi-node cluster and no case in which an automatic snapshot overshoots the bound.

The below-bound case is not expected to elect a leader, because the configuration-recovery defect of the sibling investigation is active on the same restart; this experiment only asserts that NewRaft returns, and the leadership observation is reported without being asserted.

scope.description: Three in-memory voters A, B and C on one another's transports. A snapshots while {A,B,C} is committed; the leader then removes C, which commits against {A,B}, and commits three more entries. A is shut down and restarted with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled over the same stores, while B is disconnected from A and C. The harness reports A's tracked configuration, whether A wins the election, and for a command applied after that: the client result, A's commit and applied index, whether A's FSM applied the payload, and whether the entry is present in A's, B's and C's logs.
assumptions: The removed server C keeps running and keeps answering AppendEntries, which is what a removal without shutting the process down leaves in place; the harness does not simulate C being killed.

A's snapshot is taken through the normal snapshot goroutine while the committed configuration is still {A,B,C}, so its configuration index is the bootstrap entry's index and its configuration contains C.
B is partitioned before A is restarted, so the committed configuration's only other voter cannot contribute an acknowledgement.
The nodes are in-memory transports and stores in one process; leadership, terms and quorum arithmetic are the real code paths.
excluded: No process-level restart, no production log store, and no attempt to complete the downstream loss of the entry; the predicate stops at the commitment rule.
No case in which the restarted node is the only stale voter or in which the stale configuration excludes a voter rather than including a removed one.

basis.prefix: The harness builds three assuranceMultiNode values: NewInmemTransport with a random address each, inmemConfig with LocalID = 'server-' + address and RestoreCommittedLogs true for every node, plus NewInmemCommitTrackingStore, NewInmemStore and NewInmemSnapshotStore per node. All transports are connected pairwise; BootstrapCluster is called on each node with the same three-voter configuration; NewRaft is called for each with a fresh MockFSM. The harness then waits for a real leader, applies one command through it, and takes a user snapshot on A through A.raft.Snapshot() while {A,B,C} is committed. It calls RemoveServer(C) on the leader and waits for that future, then applies three more commands, and records A's staged commit index, last index and the newest configuration entry in A's log. A is shut down and B is disconnected from A's transport and C's transport; a new transport bound to A's old address is created and connected to C only. NewRaft is called again on A's stores with RestoreCommittedLogs true and a fresh MockFSM. The harness reads A's tracked configurations through r.configurationsCh, waits up to five seconds for A to lead, and if it does, applies the payload 'stale-quorum-entry' with a two second timeout, then samples A's log entry term, the same index in B's and C's logs, A's commit and applied indexes, and A's FSM log contents.
basis.responsibility: raft's leader is responsible for committing an entry only when a majority of the configuration it is bound to has stored it, and raft's startup recovery is responsible for binding the leader to the configuration the committed log establishes rather than to an older one.

comparisons.description: Where the restart that tracks the snapshot's older three-voter configuration became leader while its log's committed configuration has two voters, committing an entry that its FSM applied and the client accepted while the committed configuration's other voter lacks it is a violation; such a witness shows the commit was decided by the removed server. Where A did not lead, the antecedent is false and nothing is claimed.

semantic_changes: Leadership is moved to A with LeadershipTransferToServer before the snapshot, because the election winner is arbitrary and removing the leader (ShutdownOnRemove defaults to true) would shut it down; the predecessor removed whichever node C was even when C led.

The pre-snapshot command is committed through A and the harness waits until A's FSM has applied a command entry, because runFSM refuses a snapshot request while its own last applied index is zero and a plain MockFSM never observes configuration or no-op entries.
Every node is shut down on all exit paths so no raft goroutine logs through the test logger after the test returns, which panicked the predecessor's later iterations.

This revision makes the case deterministic and self-terminating: leadership is transferred to A through the library's own transfer before the snapshot, a command is committed and awaited in A's FSM before the snapshot request, and every node is shut down on all exit paths. scope.description: Three in-memory voters A, B and C. A command is committed, A is shut down and restarted with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled and no snapshot on its stores, and the harness records A's tracked configuration and the newest configuration entry in A's log. A command is committed again so A's FSM has something to snapshot, A takes a snapshot through the normal path, and the harness compares the snapshot's recorded configuration and configuration index with the configuration entry in A's log. A is then shut down and restarted again with the replay disabled, and the harness records the configuration the node comes up with.
assumptions: A's stores hold no snapshot before the first restart, so the flag-on startup replays the committed log above index 0 and the scan is skipped.
The snapshot is taken through the library's normal snapshot path (user snapshot request handled by the snapshot goroutine), so nothing in the harness supplies the configuration it records.
The second restart uses the same stores with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs false and a fresh in-memory FSM, so the configuration can only come from the snapshot metadata and the log scan.
The flag-off restart is expected to run without a leader in the observation window because an empty configuration prevents the node from starting an election.
excluded: No multi-node partition and no commit-rule consequence in this case; the earlier multi-node experiment covers that.
No production snapshot store, no process-level restart, and no case in which a later configuration entry above the snapshot index repairs the tracked configuration.
The harness does not attempt to remove the corrupt snapshot, so recovery by deleting durable state is not measured.

basis.prefix: The harness builds three assuranceMultiNode values (random in-memory transport addresses, inmemConfig with RestoreCommittedLogs true, NewInmemCommitTrackingStore, NewInmemStore and NewInmemSnapshotStore per node), wires the transports pairwise, calls BootstrapCluster with the same three-voter configuration on each node and NewRaft with a fresh MockFSM each. It waits for a real leader, and if A won, moves leadership to B with LeadershipTransferToServer so that A can be restarted without stopping the cluster's leader. One command is committed and the harness waits until A's FSM has applied a command entry. A is shut down and a new transport on A's address is connected to B and C; NewRaft is called on A's stores with RestoreCommittedLogs true and a fresh MockFSM, and the harness records the tracked configurations through r.configurationsCh plus A's staged commit index, last index and newest configuration entry. One more command is committed and awaited in A's FSM, then A.Snapshot() is called and the harness reads the newest SnapshotMeta from A's snapshot store, comparing its Configuration and ConfigurationIndex with the log's configuration entry. A is shut down again, a further transport is created on the same address and connected to B and C, and NewRaft is called with RestoreCommittedLogs false; the harness records the restored snapshot index, the tracked configuration, the leader observation over 1500ms and the final state.
basis.responsibility: raft's snapshot writer is responsible for recording the committed configuration that the node's log establishes, and raft's startup recovery is responsible for establishing membership from durable state; a node that loses its configuration must not write that loss into the durable record other nodes and later restarts depend on.

comparisons.description: The configuration recorded in the snapshot metadata must be the configuration the node's own log establishes, not the empty configuration the recovery left behind.

A restart with the replay disabled must not come up without a membership configuration when its own snapshot and log establish one; a violating witness shows the loss is durable rather than confined to the replay path.

scope.description: Three in-memory voters A, B and C with Config.MaxAppendEntries 16 and no snapshots. A leader is chosen that is not A, about 3000 commands are committed so A's staged commit index sits about 3000 entries above its (absent) snapshot, and A is stopped. A is restarted over its own stores in a goroutine, in one case with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled and in the other with it disabled, and the harness waits up to 8000ms for NewRaft to return. It then commits one command while two members are live, stops the member that is neither the leader nor A, and commits one further command, reporting the client results.
assumptions: The committed log above A's absent snapshot exceeds 128 * MaxAppendEntries (3000 entries against a 2048-entry bound), so the flag-on replay needs more batches than the FSM channel can hold.
The leader is moved away from A with the library's own leadership transfer so that stopping and restarting A does not remove the group's leader.
The member stopped after the restart is chosen to be the one that is neither the leader nor A, so the surviving live voters are the leader plus A when A started, and the leader alone when A did not.
The restart uses a fresh in-memory FSM and the same stores, transport address and ID as before.
excluded: No production store, no process-level restart and no disk fault: the blocked member's process is alive but its NewRaft call never returns.
No case in which the blocked member recovers later, and no measurement of how long a caller would wait before giving up on NewRaft.
Only one extra member is stopped, so the comparison is between a two-member and a one-member live group.

basis.prefix: The harness builds three assuranceMultiNode values with random in-memory transport addresses, inmemConfig overridden with MaxAppendEntries 16, SnapshotThreshold 1<<30, SnapshotInterval one hour and RestoreCommittedLogs true, plus a NewInmemCommitTrackingStore, NewInmemStore and NewInmemSnapshotStore per node. The harness waits for a real leader and, if A won, transfers leadership to B with LeadershipTransferToServer before continuing. About 3000 commands are applied through the leader, each waiting for its future, and the harness records A's staged commit index, log last index, snapshot index and the implied replay batch count. A is shut down, a new transport bound to A's address is connected to B and C, and NewRaft is called in a separate goroutine on A's stores with a fresh MockFSM and the case's RestoreCommittedLogs value; the main goroutine waits up to 8000ms, and on non-return samples all goroutine stacks and reports the excerpt around the first frame naming restoreFromCommittedLogs. The harness then applies one command through the leader while two members are live, shuts down the member that is neither the leader nor A, applies one further command, and reports both results plus the state of the restart.
basis.responsibility: NewRaft owns completion of its own startup work, and a group's fault tolerance depends on every configured voter being able to run: a member that never finishes starting is a member the group does not have.

comparisons.description: Where the restarted member never returned from NewRaft, stopping one further member must not cost the group the ability to commit, because a member that could have started should still be available; the companion commit_while_two_live_ok field records that the group was committing before that stop.

scope.description: Two single-voter prefixes at Config.MaxAppendEntries 16 with no snapshot, built so that their persisted commit index ends at 2049 and 2050. assumptions: The prefix applies commands one at a time and stops as soon as the store's commit index reaches the target, and the harness reports the value it actually reached.
The tuple count is derived by scanning the replayed range for LogCommand, LogBarrier and LogConfiguration entries, which is what prepareLog accepts at the default protocol version 3.
No snapshot exists on either prefix, so the replay starts at index 1 and the whole range is delivered.
The block is judged by non-return within 8000ms plus a stack sample naming the replay frames; permanence comes from the source, since the channel's only consumer starts after the replay returns.
excluded: No production store, no multi-node group and no default SnapshotThreshold: the point of this case is the boundary in batches, not the reachability of the range under default settings.
Only two points are placed, one batch below and one batch above the capacity, so no finer scan of the edge is attempted.

basis.prefix: For each target the harness creates an in-memory transport and a commit-tracking log store, configures inmemConfig with RestoreCommittedLogs true, MaxAppendEntries 16, SnapshotThreshold 1<<30 and SnapshotInterval one hour, calls BootstrapCluster with the single voter and NewRaft with a fresh MockFSM, waits for real leadership, and then applies one command at a time, re-reading the store's commit index after each apply, until it reaches the target. comparisons.description: A replay of exactly 128 delivered batches fills the channel without exceeding it, so NewRaft must return.

A replay of 129 delivered batches needs one more batch than the channel holds, so NewRaft must still return; the pair with the 128-batch case places the bound at the channel's capacity in delivered batches rather than at a count of replayed log entries.

scope.description: Two single-voter prefixes built with DefaultConfig values left in place: SnapshotThreshold 8192, MaxAppendEntries 64, SnapshotInterval 120s, with only Config.RestoreCommittedLogs and the node timeouts changed. assumptions: The workload is a burst: the harness applies each command as fast as the in-memory stack allows, which is what a node whose write rate outpaces its snapshot cadence experiences.
The automatic snapshot loop wakes on a randomized timeout of up to SnapshotInterval, so the committed range above the newest snapshot can sit above the bound between checks.
The prefixes report whether any snapshot existed at restart, so the receipt shows whether the boundary condition held rather than assuming it.
The bound is the FSM channel's capacity of 128 batches times MaxAppendEntries commit tuples, which is what the earlier boundary experiment placed exactly.
excluded: No steady-state measurement of how long a node spends above the bound, and no production store, process-level restart or multi-node group.

basis.prefix: For each case the harness creates an in-memory transport, sets Config.LocalID and RestoreCommittedLogs true on inmemConfig (which overrides only the heartbeat, election, lease and commit timeouts), and leaves SnapshotThreshold, SnapshotInterval and MaxAppendEntries at their defaults. scope.description: Three in-memory voters A, B and C. A's stores hold no snapshot, so with the replay enabled the startup scan is skipped and A ends up with an empty tracked configuration; with the replay disabled the scan covers the log and A recovers the three-voter configuration.

Removing the other voters by shutting them down tests whether the surviving voter attempts candidacy, not whether it can win; with the recovered three-voter configuration A cannot win either, since its quorum is two.
The two cases use separate clusters built the same way, so the flag is the only difference.
